if you have never touched an AI agent, this is the whole on ramp in one list. no paid seats, no lock in, clone and go

> NousResearch/hermes-agent, 230k ⭐️
a personal agent with memory and tools that grows with you. a clean place to start.

> n8n-io/n8n, 201k ⭐️
visual workflow automation. wire up agents and tools with almost no code.

> anomalyco/opencode, 198k ⭐️
one of the hottest coding agents right now, clean terminal UI, many providers.

> anthropics/claude-code, 142k⭐️

> google-gemini/gemini-cli, 106k⭐️

open source coding agent for VS Code. easy if you already live there.

no subscription. no gatekeeper. one terminal and a repo.

a builder I know started on aider in an afternoon and never went back. it is all free. almost nobody who wants in has actually started.

text:
Stanford + MIT paper on Model Harnesses shows that AI performance depends not just on the model itself, but on the surrounding system code — the “harness”.

This is what decides what to store, retrieve, show to the model, and how the workflow runs. With the same underlying LLM, changing the harness can create up to a 6× performance gap on the same benchmark.

They conclude the harness around a model matters as much as the model itself. 

The paper introduces Meta-Harness, an outer-loop system that automatically improves harness code. Instead of giving the optimizing agent only a score or a short summary of past attempts, it gives the agent rich access to prior code, logs, and execution traces through a filesystem-like setup. 

The idea is that better diagnostic visibility lets the system improve the harness more intelligently.

What it found is pretty significant. 

- On online text classification, a 7.7-point improvement over a strong SOTA context management, while using 4X fewer context tokens. 

- On retrieval-augmented math reasoning, an average gain of 4.7 points across five held-out models on 200 IMO-level problems. On agentic coding, the discovered harnesses beat strong hand-engineered baselines on TerminalBench-2.

The paper shifts attention from “which model is best?” to “how is the whole AI system designed?” 

For real deployments, harness design affects reliability, tool usage, context management, and failure recovery. 

----

Paper – arxiv. org/abs/2603.28052

Sebanyak 136 siswa dan guru SMAN 1 Tunjungan, Kabupaten Blora, Jawa Tengah, diduga mengalami keracunan massal setelah mengonsumsi makanan dari program Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG), Selasa (8/9/2026).

Para korban yang berasal dari kelas 10 hingga 12 mengalami sejumlah gejala, di antaranya mual, muntah, pusing, diare, dan lemas.

Dugaan sementara mengarah pada menu MBG berupa mie bakso goreng yang dikonsumsi para siswa dan guru. Namun, penyebab pasti kejadian tersebut masih dalam penyelidikan.

Dinas kesehatan bersama kepolisian telah menerjunkan tim ke sekolah untuk mengambil sampel makanan guna menjalani uji laboratorium. Petugas juga masih melakukan pendataan jumlah korban serta mengevaluasi makanan dan vendor penyedia MBG.

Hasil pemeriksaan laboratorium dan medis nantinya akan menjadi dasar untuk memastikan penyebab kejadian yang dialami para siswa dan guru tersebut.

Gimana menurutmu?

Sebanyak 36 ribu kepala desa yang tergabung dalam Koordinator Kepala Desa Akhir Masa Jabatan (AMJ) menemui pimpinan DPR di Jakarta, Rabu (9/9/2026). Mereka meminta masa jabatan kepala desa diperpanjang sebagai penjabat (Pj) dan Pilkades periode 2027 hingga 2029 dihentikan untuk periode tertentu. 

Para kepala desa meminta agar Pj kepala desa tidak berasal dari ASN, melainkan dapat diisi oleh kepala desa yang masa jabatannya telah berakhir. Saat ini, kepala desa yang habis masa jabatan akan digantikan Pj dari ASN hingga kepala desa terpilih kembali secara definitif melalui Pilkades.

A few people have sent me the Pearl "Heresy" article this week asking what I think, so here it is. Up front, I have nothing against Pearl. The cryptography is real, the Together AI endpoint is real, and I hope it does well. I'm only here for the four middle paragraphs headed "Bittensor: The False Prophet."

I've watched this exact thing happen a few times over the past three years I've paid attention to Bittensor. Every crypto<>AI coin, every proof of useful work launch, every "AI Bitcoin," every decentralized compute token gets about a third of the way through its thesis and then stops to try to take down Bittensor first. To me, that's a tacit admission that when the market hears "AI money," it's already pointing at $TAO, otherwise, there'd be nothing to take down, and you don't get to claim the throne without at least gesturing at the king on the throne. I find it funny, and the critiques fail every time for the same reason, which is that the people writing them have read about Bittensor and haven't understood it. So I'm going to do this again, because apparently I have no choice, lol.

TL;DR: This all comes down to how you want to subjectively define "AI Bitcoin." Pearl's version of AI Bitcoin is proving that a MatMul happened (rather than a SHA-256 hash). Bittensor's version of AI Bitcoin is to abstract the concept of "mining" for hashrate and reapply it to "mining" for intelligence (which turns out to be many different digital commodities). The actual monetary policy of the currency ($TAO) is identical to Bitcoin's, and the author conflates it with the industrial policy of the network (emission routing).

Now,

***takes a deep breath***

What the author actually says about Bittensor is narrower than the section title. The way I see it, four claims were made:

>Yuma Consensus is subjective;
>validators have a track record of coordinating;
>the emission model keeps changing; 
>therefore, Bittensor "permanently disqualified itself from being AI money"

To his credit, the author does add in the same passage that this "may be completely reasonable for an AI coordination network" and that "value can still flow to $TAO." I'd ask people to keep that concession in mind - I think he's basically right on the facts and wrong about what follows from them.

The first thing I'd say is that Pearl and Bittensor mean two completely different things by "AI Bitcoin," and the article is trading on the confusion.

When Pearl says "AI Bitcoin" it means a Bitcoin-style ledger with matrix multiplication swapped in for SHA-256, so the "AI" is describing the hash function and what the chain produces is a certificate that some arithmetic happened. When I say "AI Bitcoin" I mean what Bittensor co-founders Ala and Const mean when they describe it: take Bitcoin's mining side (i.e. emit a fixed-supply coin to whoever provably does the work best) and make it programmable, so the work can be anything a subnet can define and grade, including problems that have no self-checking answer. In Bittensor's case, the AI is the thing being produced.

As a brief aside, I'll also point out that swapping Bitcoin's puzzle is a fifteen-year-old genre. Litecoin and Dogecoin swapped in Scrypt, Zcash Equihash, Ethereum Ethash, Monero RandomX, Kaspa kHeavyHash, etc., etc. Every one of them is a Bitcoin-style ledger with a different thing to grind. Pearl is one of the best entries in that genre I've seen because its puzzle is the first one whose output an AI customer might have actually wanted, but it stays inside the genre: one operation, one integer format, everything else from 2009. Pearl's ceiling is set by cryptography, meaning the very short list of computations you can make self-verifying at negligible overhead, and I don't see that list getting long. Bittensor's ceiling, on the other hand, is whatever a staked, competing, economically punished validator can grade, which is a much longer list. Also, for the record, Bittensor has already hosted Bitcoin's own puzzle as a subnet. Taohash (the old SN14) had miners point SHA-256 hashrate at it, and validators verify the shares, and for a stretch it pulled a serious amount of Bitcoin hashrate onto the network before it wound down. The business failed, which is what's supposed to happen to a subnet that can't justify its emission, but the mechanism ran Bitcoin's puzzle without changing a line of it, and it could run Pearl's tomorrow. Pearl cannot run a subnet.

Which brings me to "deemed valuable," his main complaint.

He argues that Bitcoin's work needs no judge and Bittensor's needs a committee, so Bittensor can't be money. I'll grant him the conclusion for a second because the premise is the interesting part. "Needs a judge" describes every commodity market that has ever existed, except one. Wheat trades on a grade some inspector assigns, copper on a warehouse assay, gold with a stamp on the bar, diamonds through a certification cartel, etc. That grading layer is subjective at the margin and occasionally corrupt, and nobody has ever figured out how to run a commodity market without it. Bitcoin is the one commodity in history whose output grades itself: a hash either clears the target or it doesn't, and a laptop can check, which is a neat trick and also a special case. If you treat it as the template for how markets value things, you end up where he ends up, celebrating a network that, by his own description, cannot tell a paying inference job from random matrices.

And that concession really is sitting right there in the article. Pearl's protocol doesn't check whether a matrix multiplication came from a customer. A miner can feed it synthetic inputs and collect full rewards. The empirical study of the live network from June (arXiv 2606.04819) ran the dominant miner on rented 3090s, got paid, found no inference code in the binary, and estimated something like 320,000 3090-class GPU-equivalents drawing 112 MW to multiply matrices nobody asked for. He answers that this is "the entire point," because asking whether the work was useful would require a judge. He's right, and the concession is bigger than he treats it. The network that calls itself proof of useful work verifies that a large matrix multiplication happened and takes the usefulness on faith. It has no idea, and by design can never have any idea, whether the result was worth anything to anyone.

Bittensor is the network that actually verifies useful outputs. That is the entire job of a validator. 

>Chutes (SN64) checks that the model you asked for actually answered correctly and fast. 

>Targon (SN4) checks the attestation that the inference actually ran inside a confidential enclave on the hardware the miner claims. 

>IOTA (SN9) has validators re-run a random slice of a miner's training work and check that the activations line up before that miner gets paid for the layer it trained. 

>RedTeam (SN61) drops a miner's attack into a sandbox against a live bot detector and pays based on whether it got through. 

The miner gets paid if the output was useful and doesn't if it wasn't, and nobody on the network cares how many FLOPs it took, because the FLOPs aren't the product. So if we're going to use the phrase "proof of useful work" literally, Bittensor is the one doing it, and Pearl is proof of work with a puzzle that happens to look like AI.

Bitcoin never needed a validator because checking a hash costs nothing, and the second your work stops grading itself, checking becomes expensive, and somebody has to be paid to do it honestly. Pearl found a way to keep checking free for one specific operation, which is a real achievement. Bittensor's whole design problem was the other one: how do you pay people to check whether an output is useful and keep them honest, and that one generalizes to anything you can score.

Also, philosophically, I don't think a market for judgment is exotic. A price is exactly this: a thousand subjective valuations distilled into one number that everyone then treats as objective. Nobody calls the copper price "a vote." Yuma Consensus takes a gradient of scores from a diverse set of validators, clips the outliers, weights by stake, pays for agreement and punishes divergence, and what falls out is a price for work. It's as "objective" as any other price is, meaning it's what the market says it is. Bitcoin's difficulty target is objective. Bitcoin's dollar price is a vote and always has been, and nobody thinks that disqualifies it as money. The author is asking the issuance layer to clear a bar that no money's value has ever cleared.

That being said, the real question, and I'll admit it was a real open question in 2023, is whether a stake-weighted vote converges on the best output or on whoever colludes hardest. Below are some highlights from over the years since then:

>Ridges (SN62) ran a winner-take-all tournament for coding agents graded on SWE-bench style tasks (emissions now get split among every agent that verifiably improved on the leader), hit open-source state of the art on the full 500-problem SWE-bench Verified set at 73.6% within four months of launch 

>Score (SN44) distilled a 19MB detection model that, on the team's published benchmark, beat GPT-4o, Gemini, Claude, SAM3 and Grounding-DINO on object detection while running on a four-thread CPU 

>ORO (SN15) runs an agent arena on ShoppingBench, and the paper that came out of it (arXiv 2606.10064) shows fine-tuning on subnet trajectories alone, from a fraction of one day's output, lifting Qwen3-4B from its published 18.0% base to 42.7% on a leak-guarded held-out set, matching the published synthetic-data baseline of 43.6%, while the arena's top agent (an ensemble) scores 77.3% on the same set vs 64.0% for Claude Sonnet 4.6 run as the frontier teacher

ORO, in particular, really flips the author's argument. The judging he thinks disqualifies Bittensor is the part that makes the data worth anything. Nobody is going to pay you for a proof that a MatMul happened. Labs pay for judged trajectories; that's the whole post-training bottleneck right now.

I'd also note that a lot of these rubric validators grade upon are actually objective (the patch passes the tests or it doesn't). Yuma doesn't require subjectivity; it aggregates whatever the validators can measure, and the subnet owner picks the rubric. As Bittensor has evolved over the years, the "subjective" attack really is aimed at ghosts of the 2023 network.

On collusion:  what Yuma Consensus actually pays validators for is agreement with the stake-weighted consensus, and the documented failure mode of that is weight copying (i.e., validators reading the public weight matrix and submitting the consensus back instead of evaluating anyone). It was real, and OTF's own docs concede the optimized version (submit the stake-weighted median) out-earned honest validation for a stretch in 2023 and 2024. Two fixes shipped that subnet owners can switch on: commit-reveal, which time-lock encrypts weights so a copier only ever sees stale ones and drifts out of consensus (with the known caveat that on a subnet whose rankings barely move, stale weights are still good weights), and liquid alpha, which reshaped validator bonds so you earn more for finding a good miner early than for confirming him late. The other kind of collusion, a validator pumping its own miners, runs into Yuma itself: any weight above consensus gets clipped, and moving consensus takes a majority of stake, which is the same threshold every chain has. And the subnet-level trend is toward deterministic evaluation, Docker environments, and held-out tests, so there's less subjectivity left to collude over. Affine (SN120) is the extreme case: a model has to beat the incumbent on every RL environment to take emissions, and the mechanism is built so miners can't win by running many identities, hiding decoy models, copying the leader, or overfitting one environment. Whether all of it worked is what the leaderboards above are telling you.

Then there's the claim that the "economic policy repeatedly changes."

The author is conflating two things. $TAO's supply is Bitcoin's curve for the coin: 21 million cap, 7,200 a day until the first halving at 10.5 million (Dec 2025, the same point on the curve Bitcoin hit in Nov 2012), 3,600 a day since, zero genesis allocation, zero VC pre-mined tranche, and no upgrade has ever changed that. What changes is how that fixed daily emission gets routed among subnets. dTAO in Feb 2025 routed it by alpha price. Taoflow in Nov 2025 routed it by net staking flows on a 30-day average. As of June 2026, the network is back on a price-based allocation.

None of that is monetary policy, and Bitcoin relies on the same distinction. The subsidy schedule has never moved while SegWit, Taproot, mempool policy, OP_RETURN limits, and the fee market re-plumbed the economics of using the chain over and over. Bitcoin ossified its issuance. It never ossified everything else, and nobody expects it to. TAO's allocation layer is industrial policy, governed on purpose, because a network that decides what to make has to be able to change its mind about how. If that's the disqualifier, Bitcoin in 2012 was disqualified too. I'd also add that the ossification test cuts the other way. Pearl launched mainnet April 27. By his own count, it had five activated consensus changes by August 11, including a Mixture-of-Experts soft fork that miners exploited to spoof hashrate and that got reverted 41 days later. PIP-3 proposes replacing the entire integer protocol with FP8, and he concedes Pearl "has to chase the AI stack, not the other way around." A proof-of-work function that has to track NVIDIA's numerics roadmap is likely going to be changing quite frequently over the next decade.

Last point, and for my money it's the one the article walks right past. Pearl's economics depend on what Rafael Pass calls duplex miners: operators already getting paid for inference who bolt on the 2:1 kernel and collect $PRL as a rebate. The model needs a lot of them, price-competitive, GPU-heavy, on margins thin enough that a 5% rebate matters. That population already exists and it's on Bittensor. Chutes (SN64), Targon (SN4), and every other inference and compute subnet are markets of price-taking GPU operators that have been selected for exactly this behavior since the day they launched. If the kernel really costs 5%, I expect a Chutes miner to run it (competition doesn't leave money on the table), and in that world Pearl is a rebate on Bittensor's GPUs while the question Pearl can't ask, "was this inference any good and did anybody want it?", gets answered one layer up by Yuma. He calls the first layer "money" and the second a "coordination layer," as if coordination were the junior job. In my experience, the value in any supply chain ends up with whoever owns the customer, and on Bittensor that's the layer grading the work.

Ab bottom, here is my view: TAO has Bitcoin's supply curve with a structural bid under it (every subnet lock, every registration, every alpha pool reserve is TAO), coordinating an economy where compute and data go in, and intelligence comes out. It has Bitcoin's issuance and Bitcoin's mining mechanism, made programmable, and it gives up Bitcoin's neutrality of allocation on purpose, because a neutral protocol can't decide what to build. I don't think anyone serious has claimed TAO is a bearer metal that no one governs. What I've claimed is that it's the one network where the coin's miners produce intelligence, which, to me, is what "AI Bitcoin" means if it means anything.

Anyway, if Pearl works, I think Bittensor subnets will mine it, which is great. Also, every thesis that opens by attacking TAO is a marketing campaign for TAO, whether the author meant it that way or not, so thanks for the opportunity.

Two fixes shipped that subnet owners can switch on: commit-reveal, which time-lock encrypts weights so a copier only ever sees stale ones and drifts out of consensus (with the known caveat that on a subnet whose rankings barely move, stale weights are still good weights), and liquid alpha, which reshaped validator bonds so you earn more for finding a good miner early than for confirming him late. The other kind of collusion, a validator pumping its own miners, runs into Yuma itself: any weight above consensus gets clipped, and moving consensus takes a majority of stake, which is the same threshold every chain has. And the subnet-level trend is toward deterministic evaluation, Docker environments, and held-out tests, so there's less subjectivity left to collude over. Affine (SN120) is the extreme case: a model has to beat the incumbent on every RL environment to take emissions, and the mechanism is built so miners can't win by running many identities, hiding decoy models, copying the leader, or overfitting one environment. Whether all of it worked is what the leaderboards above are telling you. Then there's the claim that the "economic policy repeatedly changes." The author is conflating two things. $TAO's supply is Bitcoin's curve for the coin: 21 million cap, 7,200 a day until the first halving at 10.5 million (Dec 2025, the same point on the curve Bitcoin hit in Nov 2012), 3,600 a day since, zero genesis allocation, zero VC pre-mined tranche, and no upgrade has ever changed that. What changes is how that fixed daily emission gets routed among subnets. dTAO in Feb 2025 routed it by alpha price. Taoflow in Nov 2025 routed it by net staking flows on a 30-day average. As of June 2026, the network is back on a price-based allocation. None of that is monetary policy, and Bitcoin relies on the same distinction. The subsidy schedule has never moved while SegWit, Taproot, mempool policy, OP_RETURN limits, and the fee market re-plumbed the economics of using the chain over and over. Bitcoin ossified its issuance. It never ossified everything else, and nobody expects it to. TAO's allocation layer is industrial policy, governed on purpose, because a network that decides what to make has to be able to change its mind about how. If that's the disqualifier, Bitcoin in 2012 was disqualified too. I'd also add that the ossification test cuts the other way. Pearl launched mainnet April 27. By his own count, it had five activated consensus changes by August 11, including a Mixture-of-Experts soft fork that miners exploited to spoof hashrate and that got reverted 41 days later. PIP-3 proposes replacing the entire integer protocol with FP8, and he concedes Pearl "has to chase the AI stack, not the other way around." A proof-of-work function that has to track NVIDIA's numerics roadmap is likely going to be changing quite frequently over the next decade. Last point, and for my money it's the one the article walks right past. Pearl's economics depend on what Rafael Pass calls duplex miners: operators already getting paid for inference who bolt on the 2:1 kernel and collect $PRL as a rebate. The model needs a lot of them, price-competitive, GPU-heavy, on margins thin enough that a 5% rebate matters. That population already exists and it's on Bittensor. Chutes (SN64), Targon (SN4), and every other inference and compute subnet are markets of price-taking GPU operators that have been selected for exactly this behavior since the day they launched. If the kernel really costs 5%, I expect a Chutes miner to run it (competition doesn't leave money on the table), and in that world Pearl is a rebate on Bittensor's GPUs while the question Pearl can't ask, "was this inference any good and did anybody want it?", gets answered one layer up by Yuma. He calls the first layer "money" and the second a "coordination layer," as if coordination were the junior job. In my experience, the value in any supply chain ends up with whoever owns the customer, and on Bittensor that's the layer grading the work. Ab bottom, here is my view: TAO has Bitcoin's supply curve with a structural bid under it (every subnet lock, every registration, every alpha pool reserve is TAO), coordinating an economy where compute and data go in, and intelligence comes out. It has Bitcoin's issuance and Bitcoin's mining mechanism, made programmable, and it gives up Bitcoin's neutrality of allocation on purpose, because a neutral protocol can't decide what to build. I don't think anyone serious has claimed TAO is a bearer metal that no one governs. What I've claimed is that it's the one network where the coin's miners produce intelligence, which, to me, is what "AI Bitcoin" means if it means anything. Anyway, if Pearl works, I think Bittensor subnets will mine it, which is great. Also, every thesis that opens by attacking TAO is a marketing campaign for TAO, whether the author meant it that way or not, so thanks for the opportunity.

Dr. Su said she is working to get more supply!!!!

Multi-agent coding gets messy when the work has no durable trail.

Puppetmaster is a supervisor and job store for developers running multi-step engineering work through existing agent CLIs and provider adapters.

It helps you keep repository investigations, audits, refactors, and implementations reviewable by routing tasks to independent workers and storing typed results in SQLite so jobs can be inspected and resumed.

Key features:

• Existing-tool adapters – works with agent tools including Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and provider APIs
• Independent workers – starts separate workers for multi-step engineering tasks
• Task routing – routes work to an available model
• SQLite-backed artifacts – stores typed results so completed work can be inspected and resumed
• MCP setup – the setup command installs MCP tools, rules, and hooks for supported platforms

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Project management for AI agents shouldn’t force you into another cloud account.

Pad is a local-first project-management tool for developers and the AI agents working alongside them.

It helps you keep tasks, ideas, plans, and project rules close to the code by putting a CLI, local web UI, and agent skill behind one SQLite-backed workspace.

Key features:

• One-binary setup – CLI, web UI, and AI agent skill run from a single local install
• Agent integration – install the `/pad` skill so supported AI coding tools can read, create, and update project items
• Terminal-first workflow – create tasks, search items, and check project status without leaving the command line
• Local web workspace – board, list, and table views give you a browser view of project work at localhost
• Conventions and playbooks – define rules and multi-step workflows that agents can load for project work

China is embedding cheaper, open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Doubao, Kimi) directly into mass-produced hardware rather than treating AI as a separate cloud service. 

This produces faster, lower-cost rollout across consumer and industrial products than the US approach of premium frontier models plus slower factory adoption.

Smartphones
 ZTE, Huawei, Honor, Xiaomi and ByteDance are shipping “agentic” phones that run on-device assistants capable of opening apps, comparing prices, filling forms and completing payments without the user switching screens. 

IDC projects AI-capable phones will exceed half of China’s 2026 market (roughly 147 million units). HarmonyOS and HyperOS already treat the phone as the hub for a connected home-and-car ecosystem.

Laptops and PCs
 AI PCs (NPU-equipped) already account for more than 50 % of online notebook sales in China in the first half of 2026, with penetration expected to keep rising. Lenovo holds the world’s largest AI-PC share (25.1 %) and has sold over 5 million units domestically.

HarmonyOS PCs now run local models for document work offline. China is also the fastest-growing slice of the global AI-PC market.

Electric vehicles
 BYD, Xiaomi, Geely/Zeekr, XPeng and even Tesla vehicles sold in China use Chinese models for voice, navigation and cabin functions. Policy targets 70 % new-energy passenger-vehicle sales and large-scale autonomous-driving deployment by 2030. 

Xiaomi’s Beijing plant already uses 700-plus robots to output a car every 76 seconds. Cockpit-driving integration and vehicle-to-home connectivity are being rolled out at factory scale.

Renewables and energy systems
 China adds hundreds of gigawatts of wind and solar each year and is building a “new-type power system” with AI-optimized smart grids, storage and demand response. 

Its electricity generation is already more than twice that of the United States, giving it a structural advantage for both data-center growth and electrified manufacturing. 

AI is used for predictive maintenance, grid balancing and integration of intermittent renewables at national scale.

Drones
 Commercial production (DJI and others) plus military programs give China the world’s largest drone output and export volume. 

Demonstrations now include hundreds of coordinated aerial swarms, mothership aircraft that launch smaller drones, and plans to fuse air, land and sea uncrewed systems into one network. The “low-altitude economy” is an official 15th Five-Year Plan priority.

Industrial robots
 China installed 295 000 industrial robots in 2024 more than the rest of the world combined and now operates over two million units. Robot density has surpassed Germany and Japan. 

Domestic brands hold the majority of the home market. Humanoid shipments reached roughly 90 % of the global total in 2025 (Unitree, AgiBot, UBTech), with prices far below Western equivalents and rapid factory-floor trials already under way. 

More than 30 000 “smart factories” use AI for scheduling, vision and predictive maintenance.

Military technology
 The PLA is moving from informatization to “intelligentization”: AI-enabled targeting, drone swarms, robotic dogs and humanoid platforms intended for reconnaissance, urban assault and high-risk tasks. 

Commercial scale in drones and humanoids supplies both hardware volume and training data. Procurement notices and public demonstrations show rapid iteration on multi-domain uncrewed systems rather than isolated prototypes.

The pattern is consistent: China uses policy, a huge domestic market and existing manufacturing clusters to push AI into everyday products and factories first, then exports the resulting low-cost systems. 

The United States still leads in the most advanced models and chips, but China currently leads in the speed and volume of physical deployment. And China with open source AI Models is giving America’s frontier model a run for its money ! 

So now they want an agreement with China to slow it down.

131 Siswa Keracunan MBG

Data tersebut merupakan hasil pendataan sementara hingga Selasa (11/8) maghrib dan masih terus berkembang.

Sembilan murid mendapat penanganan sementara di UKS MAN 2 Banyumas pada Selasa siang karena masih mengalami pusing dan mual. 

Sementara murid lainnya tidak masuk sekolah, mengikuti outing class ke Yogyakarta, atau meminta izin pulang lebih awal karena mengalami diare. Guru piket MAN 2 Banyumas Drs. Hari Prasetyo mengatakan, 131 murid yang mengalami keluhan tersebar di kelas X, XI, dan XII. 

Ratusan murid tersebut berasal dari 27 kelas yang terdampak sakit. Menurut Hari, penyebab sakit ratusan murid tersebut sementara diduga keracunan makanan. Pada Senin (10/8), makanan yang dikonsumsi murid di antaranya berasal dari program Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG). 

Wakil Kepala MAN 2 Banyumas Budiono menjelaskan, keluhan mulai dirasakan sejumlah murid pada Senin (10/8) malam. Akibat kondisi tersebut, sebagian murid tidak masuk sekolah, sementara lainnya tetap datang tetapi kemudian meminta izin pulang atau mendapat penanganan di UKS. 

Terkait pengiriman MBG pada Rabu (12/8), terdapat kemungkinan dihentikan sementara. Pasalnya, makanan MBG yang dikirim pada Selasa (11/8) juga sebagian dikembalikan meskipun sempat dikirim ke madrasah. 

"Menu MBG kemarin (Senin) yaitu nasi putih, ayam dadu bumbu woku, oreg tempe, tumis pokcay jagung dan anggur merah. Dari puskesmas sudah mengambil sampel makanan untuk uji lab memastikan penyebab sakitnya anak," terang Budiono. 

Kepala Bidang Pencegahan dan Pengendalian Penyakit Dinas Kesehatan dan Keluarga Berencana Banyumas Sito Hatmoko, SKM, M.K.M., mengatakan penyebab dugaan keracunan belum dapat dipastikan. Petugas puskesmas dan dinas baru mengambil sampel makanan untuk diuji di laboratorium di Semarang. ~~~

Sejak kampanye Pilpres dulu, saya nggak pernah setuju dengan program makan gratis yang sekarang bernama MBG itu.

Bagi saya semua program bagi-bagi uang atau makanan itu nggak mendidik. Apalagi ternyata MBG ini diberikan ke semua pelajar. Jelas tidak tepat sasaran.

Anak yang selama ini nggak punya masalah dengan makan siang pun dapat MBG. Ngapain buang-buang duit begitu? Memberi ke pihak yang tidak memerlukan. Memang beberapa sekolah menolak MBG –termasuk sekolah anak saya– tapi tetap saja mayoritas penerima MBG itu salah sasaran.

Celakanya lagi, Dapur MBG (SPPG) sudah dibuka di mana-mana. Akibatnya pemerintah bakal kesulitan andai mereka "sadar" dan ingin mengalihkan MBG hanya khusus di daerah miskin saja. Bangunan SPPG yang sudah terbangun kan tidak bisa dipindah.

Jika mau mengurangi beban APBN tanpa harus menghentikan total program MBG, tolong segera didata ulang: sekolah mana saja dan muridnya yang mana saja yang diberi MBG. Saya yakin nggak semua siswa berharap ada MBG.

Dan kita harusnya pastikan bahwa yang dibayar negara adalah jumlah porsi yang dimakan. SPPG harusnya milik mitra sepenuhnya. Termasuk tanggung jawab gaji manajer dan pegawainya. 

Prinsipnya: negara keluar uang hanya berdasarkan jumlah porsi yang disajikan ke siswa yaitu Rp 15.000/porsi. Jadi, seharusnya waktu libur, negara tidak keluar uang. Dan itu akan jadi penghematan yang lumayan besar.

Running an AI agent is easy. Giving it a usable workspace is the hard part.

BossConsole (BOSS) is an open-source, multi-platform desktop harness for builders who want to run AI coding agents alongside real development tools.

It helps you run an agent in a single workspace by combining an embedded browser, terminal, code editor, plugins, and an MCP tool layer.

Key features:

• Bring-your-own-agent setup – run Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, or OpenCode from a BOSS terminal
• Integrated workspace – keep a browser, terminal, and code editor in the same desktop app
• MCP tool layer – active plugins can expose tools for agents to use across the workspace
• Tool controls – disable individual exposed MCP tools from the Toolbox
• Multi-platform builds – downloads are listed for macOS, Windows, and Linux, including ARM64 options

It’s open-source (Apache License 2.0 license).

$CKB : Review 📜

What if you could give Bitcoin smart contracts without a bridge, without a wrapped token, and without asking Bitcoin to change a single line of code?

Meet Nervos CKB, a proof-of-work Layer 1 whose RGB++ protocol maps Bitcoin UTXOs directly onto its own Cell Model, so Bitcoin assets gain programmability through mathematics rather than through a custodian.

Designed by former Ethereum core developers, it can deploy post-quantum cryptography without a hard fork, and its Lightning layer is now in active testing.

Let's explore one of crypto's widest gaps between engineering and recognition. 👇

⚪ Nervos at a Glance

Marketplace Insight: Nervos occupies genuinely rare territory. It is one of the last proof-of-work Layer 1s of any scale, it uses a UTXO model rather than accounts, and RGB++ solves Bitcoin programmability through isomorphic binding rather than a bridge, which Messari singled out in a dedicated report. Crypto agility means post-quantum lock scripts can deploy as cells without a consensus vote, a structural advantage most chains cannot match. The clean contrast is that the recent 35% to 44% bounce is best read as a cheap, thinly traded Layer 1 rotating in a risk-on pocket rather than evidence Fiber usage has arrived. The engineering is respected and continuous. The demand has not shown up.

⚪ Mission

Nervos exists to give Bitcoin programmability without compromising it. The founding argument is that Bitcoin's security and its UTXO model are features rather than limitations, and that adding smart contracts should not require wrapping assets, trusting a bridge, or forking the base chain.

The Cell Model generalizes Bitcoin's UTXO into a container that holds arbitrary state, so RGB++ can bind Bitcoin UTXOs to CKB Cells cryptographically. State rent, where users pay for the storage they occupy, is the economic half of the design, intended to prevent the state bloat that eventually strains every other chain.

🔵 A Brief History

Nervos was founded in 2018 by a group drawn from the centre of the Ethereum ecosystem and China's early exchange industry, including Jan Xie, a former core R&D contributor to Ethereum, Daniel Lv, CTO of the imToken wallet, Terry Tai from the Yunbi exchange, Kevin Wang of Launch School, and Cipher Wang. That pedigree matters because the design choices were deliberate departures from Ethereum rather than ignorance of it: proof-of-work over proof-of-stake, UTXO over accounts, and state rent over unpriced storage.

The project raised $28 million from Sequoia Capital, Polychain, and Wanxiang, and mainnet launched in November 2019.
For its first years, Nervos was a well-regarded Layer 1 that few people used, described by its own community as an outsider during the era of new smart contract platforms and rollups. The turn came with RGB++, launched in early 2024, which introduced a way to bind Bitcoin UTXOs to CKB Cells so Bitcoin-native assets like Ordinals and Runes could interact with smart contracts without a cross-chain bridge. It drove a 55% price increase, 181% month-over-month growth in new addresses that April, and a dedicated Messari report calling it a game-changer for Bitcoin's scalability.

The years since have been building against a falling chart. JoyID wallet passed 800,000 users and the RGB++ ecosystem grew past 400 dApps. The DAO 1.1 upgrade shipped, CKCON25 in December brought a new explorer and testnet releases, and Rosen Bridge integration passed a community vote in January 2026.

The setbacks were substantial. A $3.9 million bridge hack in June 2025 followed the earlier Force Bridge exploit, damaging trust and prompting a warning from South Korea's DAXA alliance, while KuCoin removed CKB from cross-margin trading in May 2026. The building continued regardless. Governance restructured around CKBA, a Swiss Verein replacing the old foundation coordination layer, with community votes passing Vellum, a reputation layer on did:ckb, at 64.37% and an iOS Pocket Node grant at 52.8%, while rejecting several proposals on merit.

The v0.209.0 node release hardened the tx-pool and networking stack, reaching roughly 89.5% miner adoption, and a new hard fork is in planning without a locked date. The busiest surface was Fiber: v1.1.0 shipped atomic Bitcoin Lightning swaps through a Cross-Chain Hub in August, Loop In/Out and hosted LSP work progressed, Android Pocket Node reached Google Play, and a July hackathon drew 66 submissions from roughly 100 participants, producing tools like Clasp for scoped, revocable AI-agent access to Fiber payments.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea is that Bitcoin should gain programmability through mathematics rather than through trust.

➛ RGB++ and isomorphic binding. Bitcoin UTXOs are mapped directly onto CKB Cells, so Bitcoin assets gain smart contract functionality with no bridge, no wrapped token, and no custodian, which is a structurally different security model from every wrapped-BTC approach.

➛ The Cell Model and CKB-VM. A generalization of Bitcoin's UTXO that can hold arbitrary state, paired with a RISC-V based virtual machine, giving the chain flexibility while keeping the UTXO security properties Bitcoin relies on.

➛ Fiber Network. A Lightning-compatible payment layer for RGB++ assets, with v1.1.0 enabling atomic swaps between Bitcoin Lightning and CKB through a Cross-Chain Hub, plus Loop In/Out, hosted LSP, and liquidity management in progress. Currently testnet-oriented with mainnet still pending.

➛ State rent economics. Users pay for the on-chain storage they occupy rather than paying once and storing forever, which prevents state explosion and gives CKB a demand driver tied to actual data usage.

➛ Crypto agility for post-quantum. Rather than requiring a hard fork to change cryptography, CKB allows new lock scripts including post-quantum ones to be deployed as cells without a consensus vote, so the chain can adapt to a quantum threat without forcing migration on anyone.

➛ Proof-of-work commitment. One of the last major Layer 1s still using Nakamoto consensus, which has retained a genuinely loyal mining community in a landscape that has largely moved to proof-of-stake.

⚪ Token Utilities

$CKB is a state-rent and security token rather than a conventional gas asset.

➛ State rent: holders pay for on-chain storage capacity, so occupying data space requires locking CKB, tying token demand directly to actual chain usage.

➛ Mining rewards: miners secure the proof-of-work network and receive primary issuance on a halving schedule capped at 33.6 billion.

➛ NervosDAO deposits: depositors lock CKB to receive a share of secondary issuance, which offsets the dilution that secondary issuance would otherwise impose.

➛ Transaction fees: pays for computation and transactions across the network and the RGB++ ecosystem.

⚪ Key Features

➛ RGB++ mapping Bitcoin UTXOs to CKB Cells with no bridge required.

➛ A Cell Model generalizing UTXO to hold arbitrary state, on a RISC-V virtual machine.

➛ State rent pricing storage to prevent state bloat.

➛ Crypto agility allowing post-quantum locks without a consensus vote.

➛ Proof-of-work consensus in a predominantly proof-of-stake landscape.

➛ Fiber Network extending RGB++ assets to Lightning-compatible payments.

🔵 Meet the Team

Nervos runs a notably lean current team, with three names listed formally against a protocol whose development happens largely through open-source contribution and CKBA-coordinated grants rather than a conventional company structure.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Terry Tai - CEO and Director | A core developer of the Yunbi exchange, the venue that first listed Ethereum in China, before co-founding Nervos in 2018. He remains the formal executive lead through the transition to CKBA-coordinated governance.

➛ Kevin Wang - Co-Founder | Founded Launch School, an online software engineering education platform, after engineering at IBM's Silicon Valley Lab, and led the North American organization through the project's early years.

➛ Daniel Lv - Co-Founder | Former CTO of imToken, one of the earliest and largest Ethereum wallets with millions of users, bringing genuine consumer product experience to a project whose hardest problem has always been reaching users.

➛ The founding architects | Worth naming even though they no longer appear on the formal roster: Jan Xie, a former Ethereum core R&D contributor, designed the Cell Model and the deliberate departures from Ethereum that define the chain, while Cipher Wang architected RGB++ and drove the Lightning integration thesis. Much of what makes Nervos technically distinctive traces to their work.

➛ CKBA and CKB Eco Fund | The load-bearing entities today. CKBA, a Swiss Verein, replaced the older foundation coordination layer and now runs governance including grant votes and treasury design, while the Eco Fund finances ecosystem development. The project raised $28M from Sequoia Capital, Polychain, and Wanxiang.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★★ (4/5). Nervos solves a genuinely hard problem in a genuinely novel way. RGB++ binds Bitcoin UTXOs to CKB Cells cryptographically rather than through a bridge, which is a structurally safer approach than every wrapped-BTC alternative, and Messari published a dedicated report recognizing it. The supporting work is real: over 400 dApps, JoyID past 800,000 users, state rent solving state bloat at the economic layer, crypto agility allowing post-quantum locks without a fork, and Fiber extending RGB++ to Lightning with atomic swaps now working on testnet. The 1-point deduction is adoption relative to capability. The BTCFi narrative has not delivered the volume the architecture anticipated, Fiber remains testnet-oriented with mainnet pending, and competing Bitcoin layers have captured more attention despite weaker technical claims.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). The design is unusually thoughtful and solves problems most chains ignore. Primary issuance is capped at 33.6 billion on Bitcoin-style halvings with the next in November 2027, supply is roughly 98% circulating so there is no unlock overhang or vesting cliff, and state rent creates genuine demand tied to storage usage rather than speculation. NervosDAO lets depositors offset secondary issuance dilution, which is an elegant answer to perpetual inflation. The 1.5-point deduction is that secondary issuance of 1.344 billion annually is perpetual by design, network usage is too low for state rent or fees to offset it meaningfully, and the token remains roughly 97% below its peak despite the recent bounce.

➛ Audits: ★★★ (3/5). This is where the record is hardest. Nervos has suffered two bridge security incidents, including a $3.9 million hack in June 2025 that damaged trust and triggered a formal warning from South Korea's DAXA alliance, following the earlier Force Bridge exploit. Two failures on the same class of infrastructure is a pattern rather than an accident. The mitigants are genuine: the core proof-of-work chain has run since November 2019 without a protocol-level exploit, the UTXO Cell Model has a smaller attack surface than account-based systems, the v0.209.0 release shows continued security hardening across the tx-pool and networking stack, and crypto agility means cryptographic upgrades can ship without a contentious fork. But I could not verify a named third-party audit or security score, and the bridge record has to carry weight.

➛ Community: ★★★★ (4/5). The builder signal is stronger than the market cap suggests. A July Fiber hackathon drew 66 submissions from roughly 100 participants, producing genuinely creative work including Clasp for scoped, revocable AI-agent access to payments and a Cashu mint settling over Fiber, which is the clearest evidence of developer density this ecosystem has produced. Governance through CKBA functions on substance rather than rubber-stamping, passing Vellum at 64.37% and the iOS Pocket Node grant at 52.8% while rejecting proposals like fiber-payjoin-kit V2 and a mobile SDK on technical grounds. The miner base has held through a 97% drawdown, with 89.5% upgrading promptly to the current client, and community activity spans Kenya, Shanghai, Vietnam, and Colorado. The 1-point deduction is scale: roughly 70 CKBuilders and 45 tracked projects is a real ecosystem but a small one, and the DAXA warning and KuCoin delisting have narrowed mainstream access.

🔵 Conclusion

Nervos is one of the most intellectually serious projects in crypto and one of the least rewarded. A team drawn from Ethereum core development and the imToken wallet built a chain that deliberately reversed Ethereum's central choices, keeping proof-of-work and the UTXO model, then solved Bitcoin programmability through isomorphic binding rather than a bridge, which Messari recognized in print. State rent prices storage properly.

Crypto agility lets post-quantum cryptography deploy without a hard fork. Fiber is bringing Lightning-compatible payments to RGB++ assets, and a 66-submission hackathon shows builders are actually using it.
The risks are real and partly self-inflicted.

Two bridge exploits, including a $3.9 million loss in June 2025, brought a regulatory warning from South Korea's DAXA and reinforced exactly the trust problem RGB++ was designed to solve. Secondary issuance continues perpetually while usage stays too thin to offset it. Exchange access has narrowed, Fiber remains testnet-oriented with mainnet pending, and the recent 40% bounce reflects a cheap asset rotating rather than demand arriving.

But the bull case has a specific shape. If Bitcoin programmability becomes genuinely important, the approach requiring no bridge and no custodian is the one that should win, and Nervos has been building it since 2018 with Lightning integration now in active testing and a developer community shipping real tools against it.

Nervos has spent eight years being technically right and commercially invisible. The question is whether the market ever arrives to check the work.

The mitigants are genuine: the core proof-of-work chain has run since November 2019 without a protocol-level exploit, the UTXO Cell Model has a smaller attack surface than account-based systems, the v0.209.0 release shows continued security hardening across the tx-pool and networking stack, and crypto agility means cryptographic upgrades can ship without a contentious fork. But I could not verify a named third-party audit or security score, and the bridge record has to carry weight. ➛ Community: ★★★★ (4/5). The builder signal is stronger than the market cap suggests. A July Fiber hackathon drew 66 submissions from roughly 100 participants, producing genuinely creative work including Clasp for scoped, revocable AI-agent access to payments and a Cashu mint settling over Fiber, which is the clearest evidence of developer density this ecosystem has produced. Governance through CKBA functions on substance rather than rubber-stamping, passing Vellum at 64.37% and the iOS Pocket Node grant at 52.8% while rejecting proposals like fiber-payjoin-kit V2 and a mobile SDK on technical grounds. A team drawn from Ethereum core development and the imToken wallet built a chain that deliberately reversed Ethereum's central choices, keeping proof-of-work and the UTXO model, then solved Bitcoin programmability through isomorphic binding rather than a bridge, which Messari recognized in print. State rent prices storage properly. Crypto agility lets post-quantum cryptography deploy without a hard fork. Fiber is bringing Lightning-compatible payments to RGB++ assets, and a 66-submission hackathon shows builders are actually using it. The risks are real and partly self-inflicted. Secondary issuance continues perpetually while usage stays too thin to offset it. Exchange access has narrowed, Fiber remains testnet-oriented with mainnet pending, and the recent 40% bounce reflects a cheap asset rotating rather than demand arriving. But the bull case has a specific shape. If Bitcoin programmability becomes genuinely important, the approach requiring no bridge and no custodian is the one that should win, and Nervos has been building it since 2018 with Lightning integration now in active testing and a developer community shipping real tools against it. Nervos has spent eight years being technically right and commercially invisible. The question is whether the market ever arrives to check the work.

I've been paying for API credits every month just to keep my coding agent alive. Turns out I didn't have to.

It's called Free Claude Code. FCC.

It's a local proxy. Plug in a free NVIDIA NIM key, point your agent at localhost, keep working.

The part I didn't expect: it isn't only for Claude Code.

Ten agents run off the same model catalog. Claude Code, Codex, Cline, OpenCode, Aider, Pi, Hermes, DeepSeek Harness, Grok Build, Muse Code.

What it does:

- 50 ToS-friendly providers. 1.3B+ free tokens every month.
- Automatic fallback. When retries run out on one model it moves to the next one without making you restart the turn.
- Up to 90% fewer terminal-output tokens with the optional RTK filter.
- Discord and Telegram bots, so the agent runs from your phone.
- Voice notes in, code out, through local Whisper.

There's a browser mode too. Pick a folder, run Codex in a tab, switch providers mid-session.

What people pay right now: a subscription per agent, or credits that drain to zero and reset every month.

FCC: one install script and a free key from https://t.co/NsFIcKiUwk.

One honest note. Those free tiers aren't FCC's to promise. Every provider sets its own limits and can change them tomorrow. And a request that fails partway through the fallback list can burn usage on more than one provider before it lands.

MIT licensed. Independent project, not affiliated with Anthropic.

Free, open source, and running on my machine tonight.

agents are starting to use browsers, desktops and actual phones

10 repos pushing them into the real world:

Give Claude Code or Codex control of an actual phone

The demo literally has an agent ordering a Waymo from a real phone

https://t.co/jBO30RNAGj

Give basically any coding agent access to your desktop through MCP

It reads accessibility trees, clicks and types in the background, works across macOS, Windows and Linux, and can use your already signed-in Chrome

https://t.co/yi6qnBUUNO

3) browser-harness

Connect Claude Code or Codex directly to the browser you already use

The interesting part: if the agent needs a browser action the harness doesn't have yet, it can write the missing helper itself and reuse it next time

https://t.co/mVRv1xdN77

4) open-browser-use

Let your existing coding agent operate your real logged-in browser

Cookies, sessions and logins stay where they already are, while the agent can navigate pages, click buttons, fill forms and pull data through MCP

https://t.co/9QF0j88Gms

5) chrome-use

Point an agent at the Chrome session you already have open

Instead of launching a clean automation browser and logging into everything again, it works through your existing tabs and authenticated sessions

https://t.co/b48voNgMAH

6) screen-use

Basically browser-use for the entire Windows desktop

Give the agent a screen and it can find UI elements, click, type and move between apps based on what it sees

Calculator -> Notepad -> browser stops being three separate integrations

https://t.co/XOPXADarAC

Open-source infrastructure for agents that control full computers

It gives Claude Code, Codex and other agents background control of desktop apps, with their own virtual cursor instead of constantly stealing yours

It also includes computer sandboxes for running these workflows away from your main machine

https://t.co/jnu53zr8wg

Control an iPhone directly from an agent through Apple's iPhone Mirroring

Screenshot the phone, tap coordinates, swipe, type text and open apps through CLI or MCP tools

Turn an Android phone into a set of tools your agent can call

It uses ADB to read the screen, open apps, click buttons and enter text, with both Skill and MCP integrations

https://t.co/VCdM0DxbYs

10) BrowserCode

A coding agent built around having a real browser available all the time

Instead of treating browser automation as a separate tool, it writes JavaScript against Chrome through CDP and saves useful browser scripts for later runs

https://t.co/lMunlCpx6R

browsers
desktop apps
phones
real logged-in sessions

The Information reported on September 11 that Google($GOOG ) has achieved "a working form of recursive self-improvement," plans to release a next-generation model on October 5, and that internal benchmarks suggest it will outperform OpenAI's GPT-5.5 and Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8. The report also notes Google trained the system specifically on automated research, coding, and scientific discovery.

A leaked internal codename, a cited memo, a specific release date. The claim is testable, and the boundary it establishes matters more than the headline.

Google's last frontier-level Gemini Pro release was in early 2026. OpenAI's GPT-5.5 launched April 23 and Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 on May 28. Google fell out of the global top ten in July. DeepMind leadership changed in August, with Koray Kavukcuoglu taking over daily operations and Demis Hassabis moving to chairman. That backdrop defines what October 5 is: not a routine iteration, but a bet on a different dimension of competition. If Google cannot lead on the current capability frontier, it can try to change the speed at which the frontier moves.

The internal memo's language is worth reading directly: the goal is to "force recursive self-evolution, hard-convert the coding model into a fully automated AI researcher, and open up the entire R&D loop." To that end, Google assembled a code strike team led by the DeepMind CTO and directly overseen by co-founder Sergey Brin, and hired former OpenAI post-training lead Barret Zoph as a research VP overseeing RL and post-training. Brin's involvement is itself a signal: he operates from a converted microkitchen in the Gradient Canopy building in Mountain View, using founder-level influence to secure scarce compute, set priorities, and bypass approval processes that slow development.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is the first product of that strategy. On Artificial Analysis high reasoning mode it scores 59 on the Intelligence Index, close to top flagship models like GPT-5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6, at $0.58 per task. But DeepMind researcher Yao Shunyu's framing points to the real shift: "for the model, this is a small step; for RSI, this is a giant leap." The upgrade is not that it scores higher on benchmarks, but that it is designed to execute more reasoning steps on complex tasks, repeatedly call tools, and evaluate and optimize its own outputs through long-running agentic loops. The model now carries the full planning-execution-checking-repair cycle.

There is a boundary that the industry narrative systematically ignores. MIT CSAIL's Armando Solar-Lezama notes that the bottleneck in improving AI models lives in tasks humans cannot hand off — data collection, identifying blind spots in current models, judging which improvement directions are worth optimizing. Even hyperparameter tuning is "more about compute availability than programming skill." MIT FutureTech's Jonathan Rosenfeld adds a second constraint: there is a large gap in AI's observability and ability to act between the digital and physical worlds — "it cannot install or replace GPUs, it cannot debug high-speed signals on a printed circuit board."

What recursive improvement compresses is the development speed within the existing capability frontier, not the discovery of new capability categories. That distinction defines both the opportunity and the limit.

This is the part that matters most for capital allocation. Google DeepMind chief strategy officer Jasjeet Sekhon said at the Berkeley Agentic AI Summit in August that RSI is the "core investment logic" behind the entire industry's capital expenditure. He conceded that AI revenue "is not yet sufficient to support the capital spending we are undertaking," but "not betting on it seems unwise." He called the industry-wide investment "the largest scientific gamble in the history of human civilization," larger than the Apollo program.

Alphabet raised its 2026 capex guidance from $180-190 billion to $195-205 billion. Quarterly capital expenditure hit $44.9 billion, roughly double the prior year. Free cash flow turned negative for the first time in company history, at approximately -$5.9 billion. Its $25 billion bond issuance drew over $115 billion in orders, a 4.6x oversubscription.

Sekhon named the risk himself: "AI air pocket," where spending continues but revenue never materializes. That is the structural implication. RSI is not a product roadmap. It is a bet that requires validation. If RSI delivers in 2027-2028, the capital expenditure will be justified. If it only accelerates the catch-up speed without changing the competitive endgame, the return on that spending will fall short of current valuation assumptions.

Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark put a number on it: 60% probability that RSI happens before the end of 2028. DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis was more absolute: "All leading labs are heavily focused on this." On whether he fears regretting it like Oppenheimer, Hassabis said: "I worry about scenarios like this all the time. That's why I don't sleep well." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged that the company postponed a frontier reinforcement learning training run for the first time in its history — not because of a safety incident, but because "the speed of capability progress is awe-inspiring."

These statements point in one direction: RSI is moving from theory to operational practice. But the definitional disagreement is equally significant. In CACM's reporting, Nik Kale notes that true recursive self-improvement and complex internal automation "are indistinguishable on benchmarks; they can only be distinguished on a control chart." The core test is whether a qualified human verifier is in the loop when the AI makes an improvement. Google's memo describes the goal, not the current verification mechanism. The October 5 release will provide the first externally evaluable sample.

What the market will price is not the benchmark score of the model released on October 5. Those scores will be surpassed quickly. What the market will price is whether Google has proven a more fundamental proposition: when the R&D process itself is accelerated, whether the catch-up speed is sufficient to change the timeline of the competitive landscape.

Polymarket traders have given their answer: Google at 13%, Anthropic at 68%, OpenAI at 11% to have the best AI model by the end of 2026.

If the October 5 model approaches or exceeds GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 on coding and reasoning, it validates Google's catch-up speed. If it is surpassed by the next version from OpenAI or Anthropic within weeks, it validates that RSI accelerates both directions — Google accelerates its catch-up, and the leaders accelerate their lead.

The real test condition is 2027. If Google is still catching up by then, the RSI narrative will face an awkward fact: it accelerated the R&D speed of all players without changing relative position. In that case, the $195-205 billion capital expenditure will need a new explanation.

d-Matrix CEO Sid Sheth on Bloomberg talking about the Nvidia partnership: 

* d-Matrix's specialized XPUs will run alongside Nvidia GPUs over NVLink Fusion, targeting ultra-low-latency AI workloads. Deal was 6+ months of joint work.

* The logic to partner is that Nvidia is the largest deployed infrastructure base for AI in the world and he would "much rather just ride on the Nvidia ecosystem" than reinvent the wheel.

* The bet is a memory-centric architecture, 7+ years in the making. d-Matrix's edge is inference compute built around memory rather than raw FLOPs, aimed right at ultra-low-latency inference.

* Low-latency inference "just took off" in the last 12 months. Demand surged from GPT, Codex, Claude Code and the arrival of agentic coding, where users need fast compute to interact with the tools in real time.

* Lead product is Raptor, the world's first 3D-stacked-DRAM XPU. It'll launch first under the Nvidia partnership and is targeted to market in "about 12 months."

* d-Matrix uses no HBM at all. Instead of high-bandwidth memory, it packages DRAM directly with compute in a 3D stack to "punch through" the memory wall

Running multiple coding agents without them colliding is its own engineering problem.

MCP Agent Mail (Rust) is a mail-like coordination layer, exposed as an MCP server, for AI coding agents working across a project.

It helps agents stay in sync by giving them persistent identities, threaded messages, and advisory file reservations before they edit the same files.

Key features:

• File reservations – agents can claim exclusive or shared leases on file globs; a pre-commit guard checks conflicting reservations
• Threaded messaging – inboxes, outboxes, acknowledgments, priorities, and CC/BCC keep coordination structured
• Git-backed archive – messages, reservations, and agent profiles are stored as per-project Git artifacts for review
• MCP + robot CLI – agents can use MCP tools/resources or non-interactive CLI commands for automation
• Operator views – an interactive TUI and web UI provide human oversight of messages, reservations, search, and health

It’s open-source (MIT License with OpenAI/Anthropic Rider).

text:
In AI SaaS, RAG rarely fails at the model level

It breaks earlier:

▸ a contract scan turns into unreadable text
▸ a table gets cut off mid-clause
▸ the search retrieves a fragment
▸ the bot confidently gives the client an incorrect answer

I found 3 repositories that address these issues:

MinerU — ★79.3k
Parses complex PDFs, DOCX, PPTX, XLSX files, and scans into Markdown or JSON. Useful when documents contain tables, formulas, columns, or poor OCR output

Chonkie — ★4.7k
Sits between the parser and the vector database. Provides text-chunking strategies so that a random fragment of a contract clause or half a table doesn't end up in the index

DeepEval — ★18.1k
Tests not just the final answer, but individual stages: retrieval, tool calls, and agent actions. You can see that the search itself failed, rather than blindly rewriting the system prompt

A working workflow:

complex document → MinerU → Chonkie → embeddings / vector database → agent response → DeepEval checks for regressions

→ A good RAG setup doesn't start with choosing a model. It starts with the data that actually reaches it

Important: test the entire pipeline using your own contracts and reports. There is no "one-size-fits-all" parser or chunking method, and you should check the MinerU license before a commercial launch

I’ve compiled 25 more open-source repositories in the article that allow you to build an AI SaaS without a team

Setelah hampir 10 bulan menjadi penerima manfaat Program Makan Bergizi Gratis (MBG), SD Muhammadiyah 1 Trenggalek atau SD Inovatif memutuskan menghentikan keikutsertaannya dalam program tersebut pada tahun ajaran 2026/2027 dan kembali menjalankan program makan siang mandiri yang telah diterapkan sejak sekolah berdiri. Keputusan ini diambil berdasarkan hasil evaluasi internal terhadap pelaksanaan MBG sejak November 2025 yang kemudian dibahas dalam rapat kerja sekolah. Kepala SD Inovatif Trenggalek, Ikhsan Nur Wahyudi, menjelaskan bahwa keputusan tersebut bukan karena menolak upaya pemenuhan gizi bagi siswa, melainkan salah satunya dipengaruhi oleh berkurangnya waktu belajar di kelas, karena proses pembagian makanan setiap hari membutuhkan waktu sekitar 30 menit..

*Coba semua sekolah bisa seperti ini,  guru dan murid malah lebih fokus belajar mengajar 👍❤️

One web-data engine beats stitching five tools together.

fastCRW is an open-source Rust web-data engine for builders who need to turn web pages into inputs for AI systems.

It helps you move web content into agent and data workflows by handling scraping, crawling, mapping, search, and extraction through one toolset.

Key features:

• Five web operations – scrape, crawl, map, search, and extract from the same engine
• Flexible outputs – return Markdown, HTML, links, screenshots, or schema-shaped JSON from a URL
• Bounded crawling – follow a site crawl and collect pages without treating the whole web as one job
• Local or managed deployment – run a local Rust binary or use the managed API, depending on your setup
• Agent-friendly access – use the CLI, Python SDK, Node.js SDK, or MCP server with supported AI coding tools

The engine and MCP server are open-source (AGPL-3.0).

text:
if your AI agent keeps failing, I wouldn't upgrade the model first

most failures happen around the model:

bad memory, no evals, brittle browser actions, zero tracing, unsafe execution

10 open-source repos I'd use to build the agent reliability layer:

1) Langfuse

see what your agent actually did

traces, evals, prompts, datasets and production monitoring in one place

https://t.co/fDuHPiBqUj

2) Phoenix

debug the failures you can't reproduce

observability + evaluation for LLM and agent workflows

https://t.co/Cd8P2mussH

3) DeepEval

stop checking agent quality by vibe

basically pytest for LLM apps, with task completion, hallucination and custom evals

https://t.co/Q3GoHKgKUa

4) Promptfoo

find the ways your agent breaks before users do

evals, red teaming and vulnerability testing for agents and LLM apps

https://t.co/ruzIGFXfpL

5) Mem0

give the agent memory without dragging the entire conversation behind it

persistent memory built specifically for agents

https://t.co/FRo4htH9KJ

6) Letta

useful when the agent needs to stay stateful across sessions

memory, identity and persistent agent state instead of starting from zero every time

https://t.co/0GLl5pybpH

7) Browser Use

give agents an actual browser instead of another API wrapper

useful for tasks that live behind dashboards, logins and real websites

https://t.co/Dx2kgYPEoG

8) Stagehand

browser automation that can mix deterministic code with agent actions

good middle ground between pure Playwright and fully autonomous browsing

https://t.co/FmQ2OQL9Qw

9) E2B

don't let generated code run on the same machine as everything else

isolated environments for agents to execute code and use tools safely

https://t.co/9KKVHAEUMW

10) MCP Servers

connect the agent to real tools and data without building every integration from scratch

the official reference implementations are also a good place to understand how MCP should actually be wired

https://t.co/6kBbl0LGe1

the model is only one layer.

if memory, tools, execution and evals are weak, switching to a smarter model just gives you a more expensive unreliable agent.

HE TYPED "/skills" AND THE VAULT HANDED HIM A MENU.

Claude Code v2.1.201. Sonnet 5, medium effort. Vault: ~/obsidian/AzathHouse. Terminal open.

"/skill" — autocomplete drops a list. /skills. /skill-creator. /frontend-design. /run. /kanban-cli. /update-config. /run-skill-generator. Every repeatable task he's ever built, sitting there as a command.

"type skills, and"

Second frame: "find me some sad quotes. use your skills." Ten seconds of brewing. Then Mark Manson. Elizabeth Bishop. Naomi Shihab Nye. Khalil Gibran. Carl Gustav Jung. Toyotomi Hideyoshi's death poem. Asano Naganori, sentenced to seppuku.

Not a search. Not a prompt. A skill that knows where the quotes live in the vault, how he wants them formatted, and what quality threshold to apply — because he built that once and never had to think about it again.

"bunch of them."

Caption: "Use your skills."

That's the part most people miss when they build a second brain. They build the storage. They never build the commands.

A vault with no skills is just a library. A vault with skills is a machine — one where every task you've ever done more than twice becomes a single word you type into a terminal.

The quotes took 10 seconds. The skill that fetched them took one afternoon to build. He'll never spend those 10 seconds thinking about it again.

text:
Pak @PurbayaYudhi @KemenkeuRI @kemendagri
@DPR_RI 
Anda menyebut pemotongan DBH dari Rp192,2 triliun menjadi Rp58,5 triliun (turun 69,5%) sebagai “kebijakan menjaga APBN”, lalu lima hari setelah mengatakan pemotongan “tidak akan ganggu pembangunan daerah”, Anda menawarkan “skema pembiayaan” lewat PT SMI yang cicilan pokok dan bunganya dipotong otomatis dari sisa DBH daerah itu sendiri.

Itu bukan skema pembiayaan. Itu konversi hak menjadi kewajiban.

DBH adalah hak konstitusional daerah atas bagian hasil pajak dan SDA yang dihasilkan di wilayahnya. Itu bukan “uang saku dari orang tua yang boleh dipotong lalu diganti pinjaman berbunga”. 

Ketika Anda memotong hak itu secara drastis, lalu menawarkan pinjaman yang pembayarannya diambil dari hak yang sama, Anda sedang melakukan dua hal sekaligus: merampas ruang fiskal daerah hari ini, dan membebani ruang fiskal daerah di masa depan dengan utang plus bunga.

Analogi yang dipakai Ketua Fraksi @PKB        DPRD Sulteng Muhammad Safri sangat tepat: uang saku anak dipotong, lalu ketika anak butuh, disuruh meminjam uangnya sendiri lewat lembaga milik keluarga, wajib dikembalikan plus bunga. 

Bupati Siak Afni Zulkifli menolak terang-terangan karena daerahnya sudah punya utang kepada pihak ketiga dan membutuhkan cash, bukan utang baru. 

Contoh Tapanuli Tengah yang masih mencicil pinjaman SMI sebelumnya menunjukkan realitasnya: setiap tahun ada ruang fiskal APBD yang hilang permanen untuk cicilan, bukan untuk pelayanan publik.

Anda bilang ini “opsi”. Opsi yang muncul setelah haknya dipotong 69,5%. Opsi yang membuat daerah yang menolak tetap kehilangan uang, sementara yang menerima akan menanggung bunga dan risiko fiskal jangka panjang. 

Opsi yang mengubah hubungan pusat-daerah dari desentralisasi fiskal menjadi hubungan kreditur-debitur, di mana krediturnya adalah lembaga di bawah kendali Kemenkeu sendiri.

Ini bukan soal “daerah banyak uang mengendap” atau “belanja tidak optimal”. Kalau serapan bermasalah, perbaiki sistem, perkuat pengawasan, atau redesign mekanisme transfer. Jangan potong hak, lalu jual kembali dalam bentuk utang. Itu bukan reformasi. Itu financialization of regional rights.

UU tentang hubungan keuangan pusat dan daerah serta semangat otonomi daerah tidak merancang DBH sebagai jaminan utang. 

Ketika Anda menjadikan DBH sebagai sumber cicilan otomatis, Anda secara de facto mengubah karakter hukumnya dari hak menjadi jaminan. Itu langkah yang sangat berbahaya secara konstitusional dan politik.

Kalau tujuan Anda benar-benar memastikan infrastruktur terbangun, maka solusinya adalah:

1. Salurkan DBH sesuai haknya.
2. Perbaiki tata kelola dan akuntabilitas belanja daerah secara serius.
3. Sediakan pembiayaan murah atau hibah bersyarat untuk proyek prioritas, bukan pinjaman berbunga yang dipotong dari hak yang sama.

Bukan dengan cara memotong dulu, lalu menawarkan utang sebagai “solusi”.

Hak daerah yang dipotong tidak hilang begitu saja. Ia hanya berpindah wujud: dari hak menjadi utang. Dan utang, berbeda dengan hak, memiliki bunga, tenor, dan konsekuensi politik yang panjang.

Itu bukan skema pembiayaan. Itu pengalihan beban fiskal dari pusat ke daerah dengan bungkus bahasa teknis yang terdengar rapi. Daerah tahu bedanya. Rakyat di daerah penghasil SDA juga semakin paham.

Hormati hak itu. Atau setidaknya jangan sebut konversi hak menjadi utang sebagai “skema pembiayaan”. Itu menyinggung kecerdasan publik.

text:
AI coding agents have a problem:

They start coding before you’ve finished thinking.

You say:

“Build me a Markdown editor.”

5 seconds later, the AI has already chosen the framework, architecture, data model, state management—and probably added features you never asked for.

That’s exactly what Grill-Me is designed to prevent.

Grill-Me is an open-source AI coding skill created by Matt Pocock, well known in the TypeScript community.

Instead of immediately writing code, Grill-Me turns your AI coding agent into a technical interviewer.

You give it a plan:

/grill-me I want to build a Markdown editor

Then it starts questioning your requirements and design decisions one by one.

For example:

→ What editing experience do you want?
→ Live preview or separate preview?
→ How should documents be persisted?
→ Which frontend stack fits the requirements?
→ Should scrolling be synchronized?
→ What is explicitly out of scope?

But here’s the clever part:

It doesn’t just ask questions—it recommends an answer for each one.

So instead of:
“Which frontend framework do you want?”

you get something like:
“I recommend React + Vite because this is a client-heavy application without SSR requirements. Do you agree?”

You can simply say yes, or correct it.

Even better, if the answer already exists in your codebase, Grill-Me instructs the agent to inspect the code instead of asking you.

The principle is excellent:

Ask humans about decisions.
Ask the codebase about facts.

And the underlying skill is surprisingly small.

Its core idea is essentially:

Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding.

Then walk through each branch of the design tree, resolve dependencies between decisions, inspect the codebase where possible, and provide a recommended answer for every question.

Coding agents can write code. Keeping the work reviewable is the hard part.

gentle-pi is a Pi-native development harness for builders using coding agents on real repositories.

It helps you put structure around agent work by adding Spec-Driven Development workflows, focused subagents, test evidence, and review guardrails.

Key features:

• SDD/OpenSpec workflow – installs phase agents and chains from exploration and proposal through apply, verify, and archive
• Focused subagents – keeps one parent session responsible while child agents explore, implement, test, or review with focused context
• Strict TDD support – records RED → GREEN → TRIANGULATE → REFACTOR evidence when a project declares a test command
• Work routing discipline – keeps small tasks inline while sending large or risky changes through SDD/OpenSpec
• Project/user skill discovery – brings project and user skills into the workflow instead of leaving them buried in the repo

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Harness Engineering, 6 layers, 3 eras, 5 sources. Agent = Model + Harness.

Six-layer agent harness, one bounded loop. Guides feed examples in, prevents known failures. Sensors run linters, tests, validators, LLM-as-judge, catch new failures. Agentic loop in the center: plan, execute, verify, fix, retry or escalate, bounded retries, verify before done.

Memory holds state files, artifacts, decision log, what survives a run. Permissions set tool budgets, write limits, approval gates, what's allowed to happen. Observability logs traces, tracks cost, trip wires, what you can see afterward.

Evidence: same model, different harness, five sources, +44 point benchmark swing on the same model.

Feedforward, loop, sensors, feedback.

Building an agent is one thing. Getting it to improve against a measurable goal is another.

Kapso is an open-source Python framework for builders who want to run coding-agent campaigns around measurable software objectives.

It helps you iterate toward a target by designing candidate solutions, having coding agents implement them, measuring their distance from the objective, and refining the closest results.

Key features:

• Goal-driven campaigns – `.evolve()` uses tree search, coding agents, and knowledge-graph context to generate and refine solutions
• Trajectory learning – `.learn()` mines finished campaigns into evidence-backed knowledge cards for later work
• External knowledge ingestion – `.learn_knowledge()` can bring repositories and research into the knowledge graph
• Structured research – `.research()` gathers ideas and implementation references for use as campaign context
• Deployment options – `.deploy()` supports local execution, Docker containers, and cloud platforms such as Modal

It’s open-source (MIT license).
