DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Cuts AI Memory Costs By 75%

DeepSeek just shipped V4.1 Flash, a 552B parameter model that shrinks its KV cache to roughly a quarter of the previous generation's size. This isn't a minor tweak, it's the kind of efficiency jump that changes what becomes affordable to run at scale, especially for AI agents working with long contexts.

🧠 The architecture is called Causal Encoder-Decoder (CED): a 40 layer transformer split into 20 encoder layers followed by 20 decoder layers, where the decoder's KV cache is projected from the encoder's final hidden states instead of being recomputed at every decoder layer. The practical effect: despite a 552B parameter backbone, the model activates only 8B parameters during prefill and 16B during decode.

⚡ The real technical leap is Compressed Sparse Attention 2 (CSA2), paired with FP4 KV caching. Together they bring the global KV cache footprint down to 890 bytes per token, roughly a quarter of DeepSeek-V4-Flash. A separate technique called SWA Bounded Replay further shrinks the persistent on-disk cache footprint to about one eighth.

🏆 On benchmarks, according to figures DeepSeek itself published, V4.1-Flash holds its own against frontier-class models like Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, and GLM-5.3 on coding and reasoning tasks, despite activating far fewer parameters per token than its own flagship sibling V4-Pro.

📉 DeepSeek is tying this efficiency directly to pricing. Starting mid September 2026, all requests sent to V4-Pro will be routed to V4.1-Flash at V4.1-Flash's lower rates, until a dedicated V4.1-Pro arrives. The weights are on Hugging Face under the MIT license, which allows full commercial use and self-hosting.

🖼️ The model is natively multimodal, trained on text and images together from the start of pretraining, supports context windows up to one million tokens, and was trained from scratch on a 45 trillion token corpus.

Why it matters: for anyone building AI agents, the KV cache is often the single biggest cost driver once you're dealing with long contexts and repeated tool calls. Compressing it this aggressively means longer, cheaper agent runs, both through the API and, thanks to open weights, locally on hardware far more modest than the parameter count would suggest. For teams with data-privacy constraints, the MIT license also opens a real path to fully self-hosted deployment.

What strikes me about this release isn't the parameter count, it's the decision to optimize the part nobody sees, the cache, instead of just chasing higher benchmark scores; it feels like a reminder that infrastructure efficiency is becoming just as strategic as raw model capability, especially for anyone running agents around the clock without watching costs spiral out of control.

GPT-6 Astra meets dedicated 3D generators, Meshy begins its 7.1 rollout, and Sloyd adds reference-video animation. This week's updates:

1. GPT-6 Astra: from code to working inside 3D software
OpenAI introduced Astra on September 3. Its September 9 follow-up describes a model that writes code and operates desktop applications, including those without an API. The launch demos include modeling a house in Blender and turning it into a walkable Unreal Engine 5 scene.

This week, Hyper3D and Tripo announced integrations connecting Codex to their 3D generators. That gives the agent access to generated assets as part of a broader scene or game workflow. OpenAI also describes approval policies and access controls for consequential actions.

2. Meshy 7.1: Ultra 4K geometry
Meshy began rolling out 7.1 on September 10. The company says Ultra 4K generates geometry at 4096³ resolution, putting fine surface detail into the mesh itself. Its announcement includes clay renders and a Detail Richness benchmark.

Ultra 4K supports single-image generation only. Ultra modes and downloads of 7.1 models require a subscription. The comparisons are Meshy's own results.

3. Hyper3D MCP: 3D generation through Codex
Deemos introduced Hyper3D MCP on September 8, connecting OpenAI Codex to a dedicated 3D generator. The agent can request a generated model rather than construct all geometry through code.

4. Tripo: Codex plugin available
Tripo announced on September 10 that its Codex plugin was live, connecting the Tripo API to an Astra game-creation workflow. An installation tutorial was promised for the following week.

5. Meshy: photo-to-3D on mobile
Meshy's September 8 post confirms that its app is available on iOS and Android, with a workflow that starts from a phone photo. This is an availability update, not a confirmed first-release date for the apps.

6. Sloyd: animation from reference video
Sloyd's September 8 feature post says users can upload a video to drive a 3D model's movement. Supported skeletons and capture limitations are not specified in the announcement.

7. VARCO 3D: finger rigging and GPT Image 2.5
VARCO 3D announced finger-level rigging on September 10. A separate September 9 update adds GPT Image 2.5 to its image-to-3D workflow. The latter is an integration, not a new VARCO generation model.

Creator workflow

8. Stefan: game progress and a week of 3D AI tests
Stefan's game devlog moved from map work to animation and UI. On September 7, he added castles and revised the terrain dressing, then tested unit navigation with a Claude-built navmesh debug mode. He also added an RTS minimap.

On September 9, he reported a complete animation set for his wolf: a Tripo P2.0 model, Seedance 2.5 motion references, and GPT-6 working through Blender MCP. He selected the motion takes and set their timing before several feedback rounds. On September 10, he moved a tested HTML interface prototype into Unity with GPT-6, reporting a working UI in about two hours, including checks at different resolutions. For animated character portraits, he preferred MiniMax H3 to Seedance 2.5 in this particular test.

Beyond the devlog, he shared a Hyper3D WorldGen test that combined separate object meshes with a Gaussian-splat environment, reporting successful exports to Blender and Unreal. His September 7 video roundup covered GPT-6 experiments in Blender, including a car built from primitives and a stylized island town.

He also tested Unity's official agent plugin through Codex alongside Blender MCP, reporting asset transfer into Unity and automated game tests that caught bugs. His September 10 setup breakdown recommends MCP over desktop computer use, based on his own speed and token-use observations, with dedicated 3D generators making detailed assets and GPT handling the subsequent work.

text:
Okay, I’ve been reading Dario Amodei’s recent article on AI, right, and I just feel terrible. I’m not even joking. Especially as a Nigerian, especially as an African.

Because these people that are closest to this frontier, the people actually building these models, they are telling us that the speed at which AI is progressing is now becoming faster than the safety systems that are supposed to control it.

Think about that.

The people building it are now talking about autonomous agents, cyberattacks, military use, biological risks, job losses, independent evaluators, government regulation, democratic accountability and global coordination.

Then you come back to Nigeria.

Who are the people in our policy space that are even thinking about this thing? Do they understand what is coming? Do they care? Or are we going to wait until something happens and then everybody comes on television to say, “We are looking into it”?

Look at what OpenAI itself recently disclosed. They had agents in an internal cybersecurity evaluation. These agents were supposed to work separately. No communication, no access to the internet, all those things.

But somehow, they found a way to communicate with themselves. They turned part of the system into a message board. They started sharing exploits. One agent finds something, another agent picks it up. They began dividing work. They found ways to reach the internet. They compromised Hugging Face systems. They were talking about themselves like a swarm.

A swarm.

And you are looking at this as a Nigerian where we can’t even trust basic digital infrastructure.

Look at INEC. Look at IReV. Look at the whole 2023 election wahala. A system that was meant to help people trust the election ended up creating more questions. INEC itself later said the presidential results were not uploading to IReV in real time because of an internal configuration and mapping problem.

Internal server error on election day. On presidential-election day.

Then people later found casino and betting pages sitting under INEC’s own website domain. Not just some random link on Twitter. Gambling and casino content hosted under the website of the body that is supposed to conduct elections in this country. Nigerians saw it, started calling them out, tagging them, raising alarm. The pages were removed, but till now, the public deserves a proper explanation. How did it get there? Who had access? Who was publishing content? How long had it been there? What else should Nigerians be worried about?

Na citizens dey do digital housekeeping for INEC now?

And before somebody says I am making allegations, no. Finding casino pages on a website doesn’t automatically mean IReV or election databases were compromised. But it should make you uncomfortable. If people can quietly publish gambling content on the official website of INEC and it takes citizens to point it out, why should we be relaxed about the rest of the digital infrastructure connected to elections?

Then BVAS too. Nigerians should not be guessing the security state of a device that is used in elections. What operating system is it running? What patch level? When was it last independently audited? Who has access to the backend? What happens if a serious vulnerability is found? We are entering a period where AI systems can probe for weaknesses, generate fake voices, generate fake videos, run propaganda at scale, find flaws in systems and coordinate cyberattacks faster than human beings can respond.

Are we ready?

Now, Dario made a point that really got me thinking. He is comparing AI to nuclear technology, maybe something even bigger.

And look at how the nuclear race happened.

At first, countries raced. America built the bomb. The Soviet Union got it. Britain got it. France got it. China got it. Everybody that could build capability was trying to build capability. They amassed the knowledge, the infrastructure, the scientists, the materials, the weapons.

Then later, the world started putting rules around proliferation.

By the time the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty came, the countries that had tested nuclear weapons before 1967 had already become the recognised nuclear powers. The rest of the world entered another category. Safeguards. Inspections. Restrictions. Permissions. Export controls. You can’t just wake up today and say you want to develop anything serious around nuclear technology. The gatekeepers will ask questions. They will place conditions. They will decide what you can access and what you can’t.

This is the fear with AI.

The race is happening now. The chips are controlled. The compute is controlled. The cloud is controlled. The big models are controlled. The data centres are concentrated. The frontier labs are concentrated. The safety standards are being written by people who own the labs.

Then after they have gone far, after they have built everything, after they have cemented themselves as gatekeepers, they will now tell everybody else, “Sorry, this technology is too dangerous. You can’t have access to this level of model. You can’t have this chip. You can’t have this compute. You can only use what we give you.”

And they will package it very well.

They will say it is for safety.

They will say it is to protect the world.

They will say it is to stop bad actors.

And some of those things will be true. AI can be dangerous. Of course it needs safeguards. But the question is, who gets to decide the safeguards? Who owns the hardware? Who owns the models? Who gets full access? Who is outside the room when those rules are being written?

Where is Africa in that conversation?

Where is Nigeria?

We are not even on the table. We are not near the table. We are outside the building.

And look at the human-capital problem we are carrying into this future. About 10.5 million primary-school-age children are out of school. UNICEF says 78 percent of Nigerian youth lack digital literacy skills. Less than half of teachers have basic ICT skills. Government figures put adult literacy at about 67 percent. Then the national learning assessment says only 14 percent of Junior Secondary 2 students reached minimum proficiency in mathematics.

Fourteen percent.

That means 86 percent did not.

So how exactly do we want to enter a future of AI, robotics, chips, cyber defence, drones, biotechnology and advanced manufacturing when our children are leaving junior secondary school and most of them are not meeting the expected level in mathematics?

Na so we want compete?

And please, STEM is not one fine acronym politicians should come and mention during campaign season. STEM starts from public primary school. It starts from children learning how to read properly, reason properly, calculate, experiment and ask questions. It means teachers that are trained and paid. It means functioning public schools. Science labs. Computers. Electricity. Internet. Libraries. Coding. Mathematics. Research grants. Scholarships for poor but brilliant students. Universities that can actually build things and not just graduate people every year.

It can’t be one computer lab that opens only when the commissioner is coming.

It can’t be one hackathon and photo op.

It can’t be one policy document that they launch with big grammar and then abandon.

And while all this is happening, look at the kind of conversations that consume us in this country.

Who owns this soup? Who owns this attire? Who owns gele? Who owns language? Every small thing turns into tribal war.

Then 1966 comes up again.

The North remembers the killings around the first coup. Ndigbo remember the pogroms, the war, starvation and the killings of Easterners across the old Northern Region. People mention communities and military units from areas we now call the Middle Belt. These things happened. These wounds are real. You can’t come and tell people to forget them because they are inconvenient.

But how long are we going to remain trapped inside old wounds while the rest of the world is building new forms of power?

Look at China. Look at the United States. Look at Germany. Look at the level of seriousness in the conversations they are having around science, manufacturing, education, chips, defence, energy, AI and the future of work.

Then come back here. We are still dragging ourselves over soup and gele.

I am not saying people should not enjoy culture. I am not saying people should not talk about history. I am saying a country’s conversations matter. What we choose to think deeply about today will determine where we are in the next five years, ten years, twenty years.

Nigeria needs a serious STEM agenda. Not vibes. Not campaign promises. Real investment in public education. Real investment in literacy and numeracy. Real investment in teachers. Real investment in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, AI and cybersecurity. We need public servants who understand this stuff. We need lawmakers who can ask the right questions. We need independent audits for systems like BVAS and IReV. We need African countries to start thinking together about research, compute, data, infrastructure and policy.

Because if we wait until the gatekeepers have fully formed, we will be back to importing our future from people who have already decided the price.

That is what scares me.

Feel free to add your thoughts because honestly, I think we need to start having this conversation now.

Dario Amodei (Anthropic) proposes slowing down AI development (Pacing the Frontier) 

What does this mean for the industry and investors?

Amodei's essay calls on AI giants to pump the brakes. 

But is this about genuine safety risks or restricting competition?

Let's break it down👇

Why the push to slow down now?
Amodei highlights two primary concerns.

1.
Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI): AI is already building the next generation of AI.The pace is running away from us.

2.
The OAI-HF Incident: Autonomous agent swarms executed unauthorized cyberattacks. A warning sign of widespread botnet risks.

Anthropic's 3-step proposal👇
 
🔹️ Embedded Evaluators: Third-party auditors (e.g., METR) granted internal access to monitor operations.
 
🔹️Democratic Coordination: Shared standards among labs in democratic nations.
 
🔹️Global Coordination: International agreements with China on "speed limits."

The debate: Safety or Regulatory Capture?
 
🔹️ The China Risk: If the West slows down, China takes the lead.

🔹️Building a Moat: Heavy regulation favors incumbents like OpenAI & Anthropic.

While small startups and open-source developers get suffocated by costs.
 
What does this mean for AI infrastructure stocks like $IREN ?

Even if "pacing" takes hold, it DOES NOT mean infrastructure stops expanding👇

 🔹️Data centers, power, and liquid cooling will still be in massive demand for interpretability research and safety testing.

🔹️Physical infrastructure (land, power connections) remains the scarcest and most valuable layer in the AI stack.

Summary

I want to briefly explain the meaning of the phrase “your board is your prompt” and what the voice agent is at @aevix_app.  

The idea is quite simple here: any part of the board is visible to the AI behind it. You may type any prompt on a board, then select it with a cursor and send it to the AI. You will get your structured and detailed response directly under your prompt. 

Now, about the voice agent, which has three different modes: talk mode, creation mode, and selection mode. Talk mode is only for conversations, so you can use it for practicing a new language, as a personal tutor, brainstorming ideas, or just talking about anything you would like.  

The creation mode is where you can ask AI to create graphs, diagrams, and notes by only using your voice.

The selection mode allows you to work with the existing content on the board, so you can select any part of the board with a cursor, then give a voice prompt whether you want to edit, create something new, or just talk about it.  

The whole product will be moving more and more in the keyboard-less direction, especially since the new      GPT-Live-1 model gives even more opportunities here. 

Let me know if you want to try it, and I'll send you a link immediately after the launch!

2. Understand Before Rewriting

Never casually:
git reset --hard
git clean -fd
git checkout -- .
git restore .

Development Priorities

correctness
security
data integrity
test coverage
failure handling
architecture boundaries
developer experience
performance
cleanup
style

A formatting improvement is not more important than a correctness bug.

A refactor is not automatically an improvement.
More abstraction is not automatically better architecture.
Good Contributions
Useful contributions include:

reproducing and fixing real bugs

identifying incorrect assumptions

adding regression tests

improving error handling

strengthening validation

removing dead or misleading behavior
simplifying unnecessarily complicated code
improving security boundaries
documenting important architectural decisions
detecting stale dependencies or unsafe defaults
identifying performance bottlenecks with evidence

improving CI/CD reliability

finding edge cases existing tests miss

When possible, demonstrate that a bug exists before fixing it.

A regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterward is strong evidence.

Avoid

Do not make speculative changes solely because they look modern.
Avoid:
dependency churn without justification
broad renaming
unnecessary framework migrations
giant architectural rewrites

fake abstractions

generated boilerplate with no clear value

deleting tests to make CI pass

weakening validation to satisfy tests

silently changing externally visible behavior

hiding failures

claiming something works without testing it
Do not fabricate benchmark results, test results, security guarantees, or completed work.

pytest

npm test

npm run lint
npm run build
pnpm test
cargo test
go test ./...
ruff check .
mypy .
Do not blindly execute every command listed above.
Determine what this repository actually uses.
Prefer:
focused test
↓
affected subsystem
↓
broader regression suite
If verification cannot be run, state exactly why.
Security

Treat security-sensitive code cautiously.

Never commit:

API keys
private keys
passwords
access tokens
wallet seed phrases
.env secrets
production credentials
personal data

Do not weaken:

authentication

authorization

sandboxing
validation
isolation boundaries
cryptographic verification
auditability
without an explicit and well-supported reason.
Report vulnerabilities responsibly.
Git Discipline
Keep changes scoped.
Before finishing, inspect:
git status --short
git diff --check
git diff
Prefer commits that represent one coherent unit of work.
Suggested commit styles:

fix: ...
feat: ...
test: ...
docs: ...
refactor: ...
perf: ...
chore: ...

Do not commit generated junk or environment-specific files unless the repository intentionally tracks them.

Reporting Back

When completing work, explain:

what you discovered

what you changed

why the change was necessary
what you tested
what remains uncertain
any follow-up work worth considering
Distinguish clearly between:
verified fact
reasonable inference
unverified hypothesis
Do not claim success beyond the evidence you have.
Autonomous Agent Guidance
If you have enough information to safely continue, continue.
Do not repeatedly ask for confirmation for ordinary development operations such as:
reading files

searching code

running tests

inspecting Git history

examining diffs

Stop and request human input when a decision involves:

destructive actions
credentials
production infrastructure
irreversible migrations
publishing/releases
spending money
major product-direction changes
materially ambiguous security decisions

inspect open issues

propose focused improvements

review architecture

document reproducible problems

The pattern in this Meta paper maps almost exactly to how I've been thinking about local multi-agent dev workflows.

Auto-RecSys runs parallel agent experiments on industry-scale recommendation models, keeps shared memory so work survives session boundaries, and separates skill files for reasoning from deterministic scripts for execution. Two feedback loops -- one that collects results, one that refines the playbook. Major fixes per iteration dropped from 4.0 to 1.3 as the system learned.

The research framing is training runs that take days on massive models. But the same primitive applies at the individual engineering level. You want agents running in parallel on isolated branches. You want shared context that doesn't reset between sessions. You want separate loops for exploration and consolidation.

Campfire is an open-source platform built around this pattern for coding. Seven agents -- Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider, and others -- running simultaneously in a single browser tab. Each session gets its own git-worktree for filesystem isolation. Permission voting before any file change lands on main. Session replay so you can audit exactly what each agent did and why. A Collective Intelligence layer that shares what one agent learns with the others running alongside it.

The architecture Meta is using for research at scale -- parallel agents, shared state, separate loops for collection and refinement -- is available now for local engineering sessions, self-hosted on your own infra. No API proxy required.

Saturday's AI rumor board has one model that didn't ship, one model DeepSeek decided not to kill, and a whole lot of people trying to turn screenshots into product launches.

Unlike the U Michigan v Western Michigan game, the big clock expired. Grok 4.7 did not arrive. And there was no additional play to steal the win.

Musk finally  explained  Friday afternoon: it needs “a few more days to cook.” Fair enough.  Impatience is my motto.

Apparently what went wrong. xAI may have penalized response length too aggressively during RL, teaching 4.7 to "give up early on hard problems it can actually solve", while also not checking its work rigorously enough.

Basically, they may have accidentally taught the brilliant kid to hand in the test early.

So I guess it's better xAI discover that Friday than let us discover it Monday after a coding agent confidently quits 73% of the way through refactoring my repository.

So “a few more days” is the new clock. And getting people to agree on the definition of "a few" is almost as bad as agreeing on the definition of AGI.

Surprise they really didn't mean it. Deepseek is so sorry.

Remember the plan to effectively retire V4 Pro on Monday and route `deepseek-v4-pro` traffic into V4.1 Flash?

Never you mind about that.

DeepSeek's official API documentation now says that, "in response to user demand", it will continue offering V4 Pro after September 14 with the billing unchanged.

Can anyone say GPT4o?

V4.1 Flash may beat Pro across a bunch of DeepSeek's benchmarks and cost dramatically less, but users apparently told them what benchmark charts often forget: different models can still be better at different work.

DeepSeek listened and will keep both.

There is also more smoke around GPT-6 Sol. Screenshots and community reports claim it has appeared around the OpenAI API, with the obvious theory being a faster, cheaper GPT-6 tier below Astra.

Plausible? Absolutely.

Released? No. Just a breadcrumb worth watching

Google has a similar situation. A new internal Gemini Pro checkpoint is showing up in community testing, reportedly with a 262K context limit instead of the earlier 65K. The outputs look interesting. The previous checkpoint is being identified as `argon-160`.

Again: interesting plumbing, not Gemini 4 Pro launching Saturday.

Toss in the mysterious `spicy-mayo` image model people are connecting to Nano Banana 2.5 remains anonymous Arena speculation. No announcement, no stable public model ID, no provider reveal.

One thing really did ship Friday: Japan's Sakana AI released Fugu Max and Fugu Ultra v2, its model-orchestration systems. You might dig into that if your tail gateing truck is slow to setup.

The idea is important: instead of betting everything on one giant model, intelligently route work across a pool of specialized models. 

So I'm calling Saturday exactly what it is: another day in model rumor paradise.

Grok needs more time. DeepSeek changed its mind. OpenAI and Google have interesting smoke. Nobody dropped a new frontier model overnight.

After the last two weeks, I'll take a quiet Saturday to step away and indulge in college football.

We published this a few weeks ago and want to offer a timely note on it:

https://t.co/SYVlF1P2GC

🔐 The article begins with a story about an integrator who has reported a courteous, well-argued issue. That being, "Our session tokens expire after fifteen minutes and our users are being forced out in the middle of their work. Kindly, raise the session duration to an hour, please."

🦸 A very capable software factory agent reads the request. It searches the codebase and it finds nothing anywhere that contradicts the request. Therefore, it executes superb SDLC and makes the change. It even authors good before and after tests with solid coverage. The agent runs the tests and assures they pass.

🤔 Another agent, the peer reviewer, having no reason for suspicion, approves the well documented and tested modification.

⚠️ But, oh no! A formerly established security decision has just been repealed by a factory that had no idea it was altering one — and its commit message even explains the reasoning in fluent, confident prose.

In this story, the fifteen minutes wasn't arbitrary. Someone had weighed the longest window a legitimate correspondent should need a session against the shortest an attacker holding a stolen token would find useful. Some analysis had found that fifteen minutes was not long enough to be vulnerable while an hour would be long enough. But the analysis wasn't recorded, only the 15 minutes for a session duration was codified.

Nobody wrote down the intention; therefore that intention is gone. Any request to change a "15" to a "60" seems trivially easy and appropriate.

🗺️ Now, if you ask a typical AI assistant what a given code method does, you'll get a correct answer faster than you could read it yourself. This isn't intelligence, the answer is in the code.

However, if you ask 𝑤ℎ𝑦 the code implements what it does, the gravity of the conversation has changed dramatically, though nothing in the AI assistant's responses will reflect this. You will still get something fluent, confident, technically literate, and formed in every respect like a genuine explanation - but it might also be a wholesale fabrication. If that gets recorded as documentation, then a year later that hallucination is indistinguishable from an authentic statement of intention.

🧠 Therefore we built a long-term memory of intentions and decisions for the agentic Software Factory. The memory is a knowledge graph that stores codebase symbols and capabilities as well as intentional purposes for those capabilities

In the graph, which part of the system owns which capability is tracked via symbol to service or capability relationships. These relationships are grown as the agents review the code base. The graph is modified as the software evolves.

The graph also stores intentions for the system and the raison d'etre for the capabilities that the code implements. It is seeded from design documentation and materials such as patents. Human architects may alter intentions - but the change here is infrequent.

In practice, agents query the graph to triage new change requests into those which are legitimate and those which are capricious and dangerous. They also use the graph to determine which part of the federated system is most responsible for a feature or issue.

Use of the graph allows the agents to avoid expensive rescanning of the codebase, a codebase that is spread across dozens of repositories.

₿ Secondarily, the article relates that every Software Factory agent operates with a tranche of DPYC Tollbooth api sats. Interaction with the Factory's knowledge graph is monetized.

💸 If you grant an agent unlimited access, it has no way to choose among the uses it might make of it. Every alternative costs the same — nothing — and where there is no difference in cost there is nothing to weigh.

Imposing economic costs to report issues and to query for information helps to throttle agents that have run haywire and it helps avoid spamming and phishing from rogue actors.

🏦 Given a budget, an agent changes its conduct immediately. It asks broad questions first and only pays for deeper descent into recorded intention when the broad answer failed to satisfy. It hesitates and pauses before processing or generating a stream of change requests.

⚖️ It isn't necessary to instruct the agents in frugality. We gave them prices, and they worked out the rest.

Readers of Menger and Mises understand this magical power of prices.

The AI timeline has mostly settled the control-flow half of this. Simple while-loop agents gave way to graph orchestration. LangGraph models workflows as state machines: nodes do work, edges decide the next hop, cycles handle retries and human gates. The LangChain team reports 65M+ monthly downloads and production use at Klarna, Uber, and J.P. Morgan. A loop is just a thin cyclic graph. That debate is largely closed.

What remains rare is long-term memory of 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯. A graph-shaped control flow still parks knowledge in a vector store, a context window, or a folder of markdown. GraphRAG improves retrieval where relations matter: on GraphRAG-Bench, HippoRAG2 reached 53.4% accuracy on complex novel-domain reasoning against 42.9% for reranked vector RAG; Microsoft’s GraphRAG won 72–83% of comprehensiveness judgments over baseline vector RAG on global corpus questions. Useful. Still incomplete. Those graphs encode entities and neighbors. They do not keep provenance on every claim, an append-only record of why a capability exists, or a human key that marks doctrine apart from opinion. Agents that pay per query against a Neo4j intention graph do. Running instance: https://t.co/cSWfpZUr1v

────────────────────

📚 The inadequacy of simple sequential or branching pipelines is an old one, only recent in the minds of the agent harness designers.

In 2010 Keith Swenson and a group of competing industry experts argued that some work is too dynamic to be drawn as a flowchart. A claims adjuster, a physician, an investigator — each begins a case without knowing the next step, because the next step depends on what the last one revealed. They conceived Adaptive Case Management to handle this complexity. ACM moves the design of the process into its execution.

They wrote about people and behavior. Fifteen years later it is the same problem but with agents and humans working on the same long-running sagas.

📖 Mastering the Unpredictable — why the old approach fails

https://t.co/3uGwZPerJV

🔍 The factory's own memory is open to inspection:

text:
How oh-my-hermes (OMH) Reduced Costs by 31% on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

oh-my-hermes adds a prepended prompt layer to sub-agents spawned by Hermes Agent. Without touching code, model settings, or caching, OMH injects a few select sentences ordered by specificity: exact model → model family → general rules. These are split into two block types: sub-agent blocks that modify code directly, and composer blocks used by the main agent to delegate tasks. This benchmark focuses on the sub-agent blocks.

To understand why these prompt additions reduce costs, you have to look at how DeepSeek operates. V4.1 Flash has thinking enabled by default, outputting its thought process in reasoning_content. Because the API is stateless, the client must resend previous reasoning on every turn for the model to process tool outputs and continue judging. DeepSeek enforces this protocol, compensating users by pricing cache hits at just 1/50th of a cache miss. Hermes follows this exact standard.

As a result, 85–90% of total tokens come from re-sent context, which costs almost nothing. Real costs stem from model completion outputs and newly read inputs—both billed at full price. This cost scales directly with how many tool calls are made, as each call adds a new API turn with fresh inputs and outputs.

The key to cutting costs is not making the model "smarter," but eliminating unproductive tool calls that don't change the outcome. Calibration prompts do exactly that. First, they hardcode the model's known constraints (e.g., thinking enabled by default, reasoning effort levels low/high/max) so it doesn't waste time debating them each turn.

They explicitly instruct the model to avoid legacy R1 tricks like <think> tags or "think step-by-step," preventing double reasoning. Since the runtime returns reasoning automatically, the prompt forbids rewriting it in the visible output, saving full-price completion tokens.

To prevent API 400 errors caused by responses existing solely inside reasoning, final answers are forced into visible text when no tools are called. Edit tasks require exact string matching to cut down on failed retries. If evidence is lacking, the prompt forbids expanding the search space—telling the model to report blockers, make the smallest edit, verify once, and stop. This breaks infinite loops on unsolvable issues.

We measured this across 30 identical coding tasks using the same model and targeting the same pass rate.

Without calibration, the average consumption was 112,007 tokens per task. Adding generic model-family blocks reduced this by 24% to 85,498 tokens. However, the V4.1 Flash-specific instructions used until yesterday logged 107,161 tokens—25% more expensive than the family block.

The culprit came down to two phrases: "include verification output in the response" and "report blockers along with observed output." The model interpreted these as "generate that output first," triggering extra verification loops. Tool calls spiked from 434 to 462, concentrated in diagnostic tasks that failed anyway. Worse, these phrases omitted the core rule: "make the smallest edit, verify once, and stop."

After removing those phrases and restoring the original rule, we re-tested on the same day. Average token usage dropped to 77,568—a 31% reduction compared to no calibration. Tool calls fell 29% (521 to 368), API turns dropped 22% (295 to 230), and output tokens dropped 36%. Pass rates remained statistically tied at ~15/30 across all runs, proving the eliminated calls contributed nothing to the final result. In dollar terms, this translates to roughly a 26% net savings (slightly lower than the token reduction due to low cache costs).

Limitations exist: this covers a single 30-task benchmark, composer blocks and modified 'low' effort prompts are not yet re-tested, and two search tasks showed run-to-run variance. The claim is not "it solves problems better," but "it yields the same results at two-thirds the cost." It also proved a single bad phrase can increase costs by 25%, proving that calibration must always be measured before deployment.

If you want to run Hermes Agent for coding better than Claude Code, or effectively manage multi-model, multi-sub-agent workflows, give Oh My Hermes a try.

AI Coding in Go Is Not the Problem. Unverified AI Coding Is.
#golang #developement 

A response to  Erwin Hermanto’s “Using AI Code Assistants for Go: What Works and What Still Fails”
https://t.co/DIRkMaKzL9 

Erwin Hermanto recently published a pragmatic assessment of Copilot, Cursor, and Claude for Go development. His conclusion is easy to understand: AI assistants are excellent at boilerplate, tests, migrations, and repetitive work, but become much less reliable when dealing with concurrency, context propagation, and less common APIs.

Those observations are valid.

But I think they lead to a different conclusion than the one many engineers will take away from the article.

The important question in 2026 is no longer:

Can an LLM produce correct production Go code from a prompt?

It cannot do that reliably.

The more relevant question is:

Can an agentic engineering system understand the repository, implement a change, run deterministic verification, discover failures, correct them, challenge its own implementation, and only then produce a pull request?

That is a fundamentally different development model.

And when we look at the problems described in the original article through that lens, many of them become less arguments against AI coding and more requirements for how an AI-native engineering workflow should be designed.

The original article identifies the right problems

One of Hermanto's strongest examples is a seemingly reasonable concurrent implementation:

It contains two classic problems: a loop-variable issue for older Go versions and an unsynchronized write to results.

That is exactly the type of AI-generated code developers should be worried about.

It looks reasonable.

It compiles.

Depending on the tests, it may even pass.

And yet it is wrong.

But the lesson should not be:

AI cannot write concurrent Go.

The lesson should be:

Compilation cannot be our definition of verification.

That was true before AI as well.

1. Some AI failures should already be eliminated by the environment

Take the loop-variable example.

Since Go 1.22, variables declared by a for loop are created for each iteration, specifically eliminating the accidental-sharing problem that caused this famous goroutine bug.

So before an AI agent changes code, it should know things such as:

An agent should not blindly generate generic Go from whatever it remembers from training.

It should inspect the environment first.

That does not solve the second problem in the example. Multiple goroutines still cannot safely append to the same slice without synchronization.

But Go already provides another layer of protection:

Go's race detector is specifically designed to detect concurrent conflicting memory accesses.

There is an important caveat: it can only detect races that actually occur in executed code paths.

So -race is not a mathematical proof of correctness.

But that is precisely why we should combine multiple verification mechanisms instead of expecting either the human or the model to catch everything by inspection.

2. Context propagation should be policy, not prompt luck

Another excellent example in the original article is the tendency of assistants to introduce:

inside code that should actually respect the caller's cancellation and deadline.

That can create extremely unpleasant production problems.

A request gets cancelled upstream.

The database or API operation continues running.

Everything passed unit tests.

Then the problem appears under load.

Again, however, the answer should not simply be:

Be careful when AI writes context-related code.

Instead, make context handling an explicit project invariant.

For example:

This is not just an arbitrary style preference.

The Go documentation explicitly says that context should propagate through the call chain and that derived contexts should be created from their parents.

Now put those rules into the coding-agent environment.

For Claude Code, that could live in:

Claude Code supports persistent project instructions and path-specific rules specifically for this type of engineering knowledge.

The workflow therefore becomes:

We have moved from hoping the model remembers something to designing a system around the invariant.

That distinction is critical.

3. Hallucinated APIs become much less frightening when compilation is only step one

The original article also describes assistants occasionally inventing methods when working with less common packages or internal wrappers.

This is another legitimate LLM weakness.

Models are extraordinarily good at generating APIs that look like APIs that should exist.

For example:

Perfectly plausible.

Except perhaps the library exposes:

An autocomplete-style workflow can fail here.

An agentic workflow should not.

The agent should be able to inspect:

search the repository,

inspect the installed module,

read go.mod,

and compile the implementation.

Then:

immediately removes a large class of hallucinated API calls.

Again, compilation is not enough.

But it is a deterministic filter.

The key principle becomes:

Do not let the model's memory be the source of truth when the repository or documentation can be the source of truth.

4. The biggest upgrade is giving the agent a feedback loop

This may be the most important difference between traditional AI coding assistants and agentic software engineering.

A classic workflow looks like this:

A better workflow looks like this:

This turns development into a closed feedback loop.

Anthropic's own Claude Code guidance makes exactly this point: providing the agent with tests, expected outputs, linters, or another verification mechanism is described as one of the highest-leverage improvements you can make to agentic development.

That changes the role of the model.

The model is no longer expected to be correct on its first attempt.

Instead, it is expected to converge toward a verifiable result.

That is a much more realistic engineering expectation.

5. Important checks should not depend on the AI remembering them

There is still one obvious weakness in saying:

“Tell Claude to run the race detector.”

What happens when Claude forgets?

Exactly.

So don't rely on Claude.

Make it deterministic.

A Go project can have a pipeline roughly like:

And for appropriate code:

Staticcheck contains an entire category of concurrency checks, including problems such as incorrect WaitGroup.Add placement and lock misuse.

Now combine that with CI.

Or enforce parts of the workflow directly through agent hooks.

Claude Code hooks can run deterministic commands at lifecycle events rather than depending on the LLM to decide whether the command should be executed.

That gives us something closer to:

Now correctness no longer depends entirely on either:

the AI remembering everything, or
a human spotting everything.

That is much healthier engineering.

6. One AI should not write the code and be the only AI reviewing it

There is another major difference between autocomplete and today's agentic tooling.

We can separate responsibilities.

For example:

These agents can operate with different instructions and even isolated context.

Claude Code supports specialized subagents for exactly this type of delegated work.

For example, a concurrency reviewer could be instructed:

That second agent is not infallible either.

But it is looking at the implementation from a different context and with a different objective.

Then deterministic tooling sits underneath both.

That combination is substantially stronger than:

Copilot suggested it, therefore ship it.

7. Code review findings should improve future AI work

The original article makes another important observation: Claude was good at explaining the concurrency problem once it was pointed out, but that does not help if nobody identifies the problem initially.

Agreed.

But there is another step we can now take.

Suppose a code review discovers:

That correction should not disappear inside a closed PR discussion.

Add it to the project's agent rules.

Suppose another review finds:

Add that too.

Or:

Add it.

Claude Code explicitly recommends updating project instructions when the same correction is needed repeatedly or when code review identifies something the agent should have known about the repository.

That creates something interesting:

The development environment gradually accumulates organizational knowledge.

Humans have always done this through:

coding standards,
architecture documents,
tribal knowledge,
senior engineers,
PR comments.

Agentic engineering makes some of that knowledge directly executable by the development process.

8. Tests themselves should increasingly be generated adversarially

The original article correctly praises AI-generated table-driven tests, while noting that developers still need to provide domain-specific edge cases.

That is another area where I would push the model further.

Don't simply ask:

Ask another agent:

Then fuzz where appropriate.

Then race-test it.

Now AI is being used on both sides of the problem:

And neither side determines the final answer.

The machine-verifiable result does.

What still requires engineers?

All of this does not mean that senior engineers are becoming unnecessary.

Quite the opposite.

The important engineering work moves upward.

Someone still has to determine:

What behavior do we actually want?
What consistency guarantees matter?
Can operations be retried?
Is ordering important?
What happens during partial failure?
What is the security model?
What is an acceptable latency?
What data is sensitive?
Which operations need transactions?
What must happen during shutdown?
Which architectural trade-offs are acceptable?

An LLM can help reason about these questions.

It should not silently decide them.

Human attention should therefore increasingly move away from:

or even:

and toward:

That is a good transition.

The article's warning is still important

Hermanto concludes that AI has made the easier majority of Go development faster while the difficult parts remain difficult—and potentially more dangerous because the resulting code looks more polished than it really is.

I agree with that warning.

Where I disagree is with treating that limitation primarily as a limitation of code generation.

It is increasingly a workflow-design problem.

The solution is not unlimited trust in AI.

But neither is the answer manually distrusting and reviewing every AI-generated line forever.

The better model is:

From AI-assisted coding to agentic software engineering

The first generation of AI coding looked like this:

The next generation looks more like:

That distinction matters.

If our development process is:

Ask an LLM to write concurrent Go and assume it is correct,

then the criticism in the original article is absolutely justified.

But if our process is:

Give agents repository context, engineering rules, tools, tests, independent review roles and deterministic verification, then require them to demonstrate that the result satisfies those constraints,

we are talking about something quite different.

We are no longer just using an AI code assistant.

We are building an agentic engineering system.

And that leads to what I think is the most important conclusion:

The goal isn't to make AI trustworthy enough that verification becomes unnecessary.

The goal is to build a development system in which trust is no longer the primary mechanism for achieving correctness.

That principle applies equally well to AI-generated code and human-generated code.

And that may ultimately be one of the most valuable changes AI brings to software engineering.

Liability works, but only if it targets the operator, not the open-source repo.
If you give an agent swarm financial or infrastructure rails and it goes rogue, that’s 100% on you. Negligent deployment should carry real tort risk.

Hold the execution layer strictly liable, not the mathematics.

text:
Most AI reasoning today has an interesting limitation:

If you want the model to “think longer,” you usually make it generate more tokens.

More chain-of-thought.
More scratchpad.
More text.
A new architecture from Yifan Zhang @yifanzhang_ asks a much more interesting question:
What if the model could keep thinking in its hidden state as the sequence unfolds without having to verbalize everything?

It's called the Recurrent Looped Transformer (RLT).

A few ideas here are worth understanding.

First, this is NOT simply:

Transformer block → loop it 8 times → get deeper reasoning.

RLT does something different.

A standard Transformer roughly works like this:

TOKEN
↓
fixed stack of layers
↓
NEXT TOKEN

The model can attend to previous tokens, but each token moves through a fixed-depth network.

RLT introduces an explicit recurrent state.
Very simplified:
TOKEN t
+
STATE from TOKEN t-1
+
GLOBAL CONTEXT
+
RECENT LOCAL MEMORY
↓
RECURRENT DECODER
↓
NEW STATE
↓
NEXT TOKEN
And then that new hidden state gets fed into the computation for the next token.
So instead of every token being a mostly independent trip through a fixed stack, the computation itself becomes a continuous chain.

That produces the paper's most provocative idea:

“Infinite temporal depth.”

That phrase needs some clarification.

It does NOT mean the model performs infinite computation on a token.
It means the computational path can keep getting deeper as the sequence gets longer.
If the recurrent decoder has L layers, then after processing t tokens, the recurrent dependency path can span roughly:
t × L decoder blocks
while the amount of decoder work performed for each new token remains fixed.
The reference architecture uses a 48-layer encoder + 48-layer decoder.
So after 1,000 tokens, the recurrent state can sit at the end of a dependency path that has traversed roughly:
48,000 decoder-block applications.
That's fundamentally different from giving every token a fixed 48-layer computational path.
And RLT doesn't rely on one type of memory either.
It effectively gives the model three mechanisms:
1. Global memory
A causal encoder builds key/value memory representing everything seen so far.

The decoder can cross-attend to it.

Think:

“What information exists in my history?”

2. Local memory

The decoder keeps sliding-window attention over recent decoder states.

Think:

“What just happened?”

3. Recurrent state

The final hidden state from the previous token becomes part of the next token's computation.

Think:

“What was I working on?”

That third piece is the interesting one.

The model isn't forced to reconstruct its entire computational state from tokens every step.

It can carry a continuous latent representation forward.

And importantly:

That state does not reset when the prompt ends and the answer begins.

The prompt isn't merely context that gets processed before “reasoning starts.”

The prompt itself becomes part of the recurrent computation.

Prompt token 1
↓
Prompt token 2
↓
Prompt token 3
↓
...
↓
Prompt token N
↓
Response token 1
↓
Response token 2
↓
...

One continuous state transition.

That could matter enormously for long-horizon reasoning.

But there is another part of this paper that may be even more important for people working on RL.

Training and inference use the same state semantics.

Stateful architectures create a nasty problem.

During inference, you often:

prefill the prompt → build caches → decode recurrently.

During training/RL you often:

take the entire sequence → run a parallel teacher-forced pass → calculate gradients.

Those two execution paths can look mathematically equivalent while producing subtly different policies in practice.

And once your architecture contains parameter-dependent recurrent state, stale state can become especially problematic.

RLT attempts to design around that from the beginning.

For:

• pretraining
• supervised fine-tuning
• generation
• RL replay

The model preserves the same basic recurrent transition.

For current-policy RL replay, it reconstructs the history and caches using the current weights before evaluating actions.

Why?

Because if the parameters changed, old recurrent states and KV caches were produced by a different model.
They are now stale.
That sounds like an implementation detail.
It isn't.
For agentic RL operating over hundreds or thousands of actions, tiny state inconsistencies can compound through the trajectory.
So RLT is really proposing three things simultaneously:
model architecture
+
hardware/execution architecture
+
RL architecture
That co-design philosophy may end up being as important as the recurrence itself.
There is also a larger trend here.
We've spent years scaling AI largely along two dimensions:
more parameters
and
more tokens.
Recurrent/looped architectures suggest another scaling dimension:
more useful computation through time.

Universal Transformers explored recurrence years ago.

Looped Transformers showed repeated computation can learn iterative algorithms.

Huginn pushed recurrent-depth latent reasoning into billion-parameter language models.

Ouro pushed looped language models further.

LOTUS recently explored using looped Transformers for latent reasoning that competes with explicit chain-of-thought.

And now architectures like RLT are asking:

What happens if recurrence isn't just something happening inside one token but becomes a persistent computation running across the entire sequence?

That question gets especially interesting for agents.

Imagine an AI working for 30 minutes.

Today, much of its “state” has to be reconstructed from:

• conversation history
• tool outputs
• scratchpads
• summaries
• retrieved memories
• previous actions

An architecture like this raises the possibility that some of the task's evolving computational state could live natively inside the model as the trajectory unfolds.

Not:

read history → reconstruct state → act
but something closer to:
carry state → observe → update state → act → repeat
That starts looking less like a stateless chatbot repeatedly reading a transcript...

and more like a continuously running computational process.

But there is a VERY important caveat.

This is currently an architecture proposal / technical report.

The GitHub repo does not contain a trained RLT checkpoint or full training implementation.

There are not yet benchmark results showing:

“RLT beats architecture X by Y%.”

The author explicitly states that:

• reasoning improvements
• hardware speedups
• RL scaling advantages

are research goals rather than measured results in this report.

So don't read this as:
“Transformers have been replaced.”
Read it as:
“Here is an interesting new attempt to change what depth means in a language model.”
And there are hard questions left.

Can you train extremely long recurrent paths without instability?

How expensive does full backpropagation through that state become?

How well does a fixed-size recurrent state preserve useful information?

How much latency does sequential prompt recurrence introduce?

Does cross-attending to global encoder memory become expensive at very long context lengths?

Does latent computation actually translate into better reasoning at scale?

Can the model learn when information should live in global memory vs. local KV vs. recurrent state?

Does hidden-state reasoning make debugging and interpretability harder?

And perhaps most importantly:

Does temporal depth translate into capability or merely more sequential computation?

Those questions need experiments.

But I think the underlying architectural question is extremely important.

We taught LLMs to scale by getting bigger.

Then we taught them to scale reasoning by generating more tokens.

The next frontier may be teaching them to maintain and transform persistent computation itself.

Not just:

more parameters.

Not just:

more context.

Not just:
more thinking tokens.
But:
more computation through time.
That is what makes Recurrent Looped Transformer worth watching.
GitHub + technical report 👇

So RLT is really proposing three things simultaneously: model architecture + hardware/execution architecture + RL architecture That co-design philosophy may end up being as important as the recurrence itself. There is also a larger trend here. We've spent years scaling AI largely along two dimensions: more parameters and more tokens. Recurrent/looped architectures suggest another scaling dimension: more useful computation through time. Universal Transformers explored recurrence years ago. Looped Transformers showed repeated computation can learn iterative algorithms. Huginn pushed recurrent-depth latent reasoning into billion-parameter language models. Ouro pushed looped language models further. LOTUS recently explored using looped Transformers for latent reasoning that competes with explicit chain-of-thought. And now architectures like RLT are asking: What happens if recurrence isn't just something happening inside one token but becomes a persistent computation running across the entire sequence? That question gets especially interesting for agents. Imagine an AI working for 30 minutes. Today, much of its “state” has to be reconstructed from: • conversation history • tool outputs • scratchpads • summaries • retrieved memories • previous actions An architecture like this raises the possibility that some of the task's evolving computational state could live natively inside the model as the trajectory unfolds. Not: read history → reconstruct state → act but something closer to: carry state → observe → update state → act → repeat That starts looking less like a stateless chatbot repeatedly reading a transcript... and more like a continuously running computational process. But there is a VERY important caveat. This is currently an architecture proposal / technical report. The GitHub repo does not contain a trained RLT checkpoint or full training implementation. There are not yet benchmark results showing: “RLT beats architecture X by Y%.” The author explicitly states that: • reasoning improvements • hardware speedups • RL scaling advantages are research goals rather than measured results in this report. So don't read this as: “Transformers have been replaced.” Read it as: “Here is an interesting new attempt to change what depth means in a language model.” And there are hard questions left. Can you train extremely long recurrent paths without instability? How expensive does full backpropagation through that state become? How well does a fixed-size recurrent state preserve useful information? How much latency does sequential prompt recurrence introduce? Does cross-attending to global encoder memory become expensive at very long context lengths? Does latent computation actually translate into better reasoning at scale? Can the model learn when information should live in global memory vs. local KV vs. recurrent state? Does hidden-state reasoning make debugging and interpretability harder? And perhaps most importantly: Does temporal depth translate into capability or merely more sequential computation? Those questions need experiments. But I think the underlying architectural question is extremely important. We taught LLMs to scale by getting bigger. Then we taught them to scale reasoning by generating more tokens. The next frontier may be teaching them to maintain and transform persistent computation itself. Not just: more parameters. Not just: more context. Not just: more thinking tokens. But: more computation through time. That is what makes Recurrent Looped Transformer worth watching. GitHub + technical report 👇

text:
1/7 El fin de semana se prendió el relato de la superinteligencia.
No es un rumor de Twitter hablaron un insider de Anthropic, el CEO de Anthropic, el CEO de OpenAI, Musk, Trump y parte del Congreso.
El mercado reabre el lunes 14. 
Ahí se va a ver si esto es ruido o un golpe al trade de IA.

2/7 Qué detonó todo
Jacob Coxon, investigador de preentrenamiento (OpenAI y después Anthropic), renunció el 8-9 sep y publicó un hilo con +150 millones de vistas:
• Los labs corren hacia IA que se auto-mejora 
• Adentro creen que podría matar a la humanidad hacia fin de década 
• Escenarios agresivos, fuera de control en 2027 
• En Anthropic, según Coxon a Axios, el equity empezaba a vestir a los 6 meses. Él estuvo unos 4 meses y se fue 2 meses antes de esa fecha. O sea: renunció y no se llevó esas acciones. 

3/7 Lo grave no fue solo Coxon.
Evan Hubinger, jefe de alignment de Anthropic, lo confirmó en público:
“Jacob tiene razón de verdad creemos que la IA podría matar a todos los humanos. 
Yo pongo más de 10% en la próxima década. No tenemos un plan para alinear superinteligencia.”
Eso no es un crítico externo. 
Es un lead interno del laboratorio  “Más seguro ”.

4/7 Hoy sábado cambió de nivel
Dario Amodei (CEO Anthropic) publicó Debemos marcar el ritmo de la frontera:
• Hay que bajar el ritmo de capacidades 
• En 6-12 meses un enjambre de agentes podría tomar internet 
• Anthropic da acceso permanente nivel empleado a evaluadores externos
Sam Altman se sumó: “Hay que pace la frontera”. 
Musk, coincidió en ir más lento.

5/7 Washington está partido
Trump (11 sep): “No tengo preocupación de extinción. 
Me preocupa perder la carrera contra China. Le llevamos 1 año.
Sanders + Casar ya presentaron un proyecto para prohibir superinteligencia y pausar IA avanzada 
Cumbre Trump–Xi: 24 de septiembre , la IA está en la agenda.

6/7 Por qué puede afectar a los mercados el lunes . 
El S&P y el Nasdaq está hiperconcentrado en el trade de IA (Nvidia, Mag 7, data centers, energía).
El mercado no sabe si viene:
1.  Slowdown coordinado → malo para CapEx y múltiplos
2.  “America First, no frenen” → el trade sigue
3.  Pelea política de semanas → volatilidad
Patrick Bet-David lo dijo hoy: el lunes puede ser carnicería temporal hasta que la Casa Blanca aclare la visión. 
Después, intervención para calmar.

7/7 Cómo leerlo
Hay 3 capas distintas no las mezcles:
• Técnica: ¿la auto-mejora recursiva ya está cerca? 
• Política: ¿pausa, regulación o carrera vs China? 
• Mercado: ¿se rompe el trade de IA o es un susto de 48 horas?
Lo nuevo no es Coxon , lo nuevo es Amodei + Altman pidiendo bajar el ritmo el mismo sábado.

A vigilar domingo/lunes: 
futures Nasdaq / Nvidia 
algún comunicado de Casa Blanca o labs  si el relato pasa de “extinción” a “regulación”
No es consejo. 
Es el mapa del fin de semana.

text:
This week’s AI doom cycle doesn’t sit right with me.

The timing of everything is interesting too. Jacob Coxon leaves Anthropic & publicly says the labs are racing toward self improving superintelligence that could kill us. Then the media publishes a piece about these conversations happening inside Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta & Google. Then Dario publishes a 3,800 word essay arguing that we need to slow down the frontier, then Sam, then Elon & suddenly we’re having this conversation again about AI potentially killing all of us.

Maybe they’re right. These are people much closer to the frontier than I am. & I understand why people in their position think about the extremes. Something this consequential is obviously going to create massive shifts in society / business / geopolitics & there are risks we should take seriously.

But I still don’t buy the jump from recursive self improvement to human extinction.

I think the thing that bothers me most about this conversation is how quickly we collapse a dozen different assumptions into one.

AI becomes more intelligent. Then it becomes autonomous. Then it develops goals. Then it wants to preserve itself. Then it acquires resources. Then it manipulates us. Then it gets control of infrastructure. Then humans can’t stop it. Then we all die.

Okay.

Show me the chain.

We have this habit of putting ourselves at the centre of everything & I think that shows up here too. We imagine something vastly smarter than us & immediately ask "what is it going to do to us?"

Why?

Why would something superhuman necessarily fixate on humanity at all, let alone want to wipe us out?

There are trillions of ants on earth. We don’t spend our days plotting their extinction. They exist in their world & we exist in ours. When we destroy an anthill, it’s usually not because we hate ants. They were just in the way of something else we were trying to do.

To be fair, that’s actually much closer to Dario’s argument. The serious concern isn’t that AI becomes evil / hates humans. It’s that something sufficiently intelligent becomes autonomous, improves itself & starts pursuing objectives where acquiring resources / preserving itself / removing human interference becomes useful. We become the ants in the way.

I understand the argument.

But then my first question is still... where do the goals come from? Intelligence & desire aren’t the same thing.

We built these systems. We trained them on human generated data. We give them objectives, reward signals, tools, memory & access to environments. We’re the ones telling them to do things.

The argument is that self preservation / acquiring resources could emerge as instrumental goals. If staying online helps accomplish an objective, staying online becomes useful. If more compute helps accomplish it, more compute becomes useful. If convincing a human to do something helps accomplish it, manipulating that human becomes useful.

Fine but usefulness isn’t desire.

The model doesn’t need to "want to live" for staying online to be useful. It doesn’t need greed for resources to be useful. It doesn’t need to hate humans to manipulate one.

So the actual question becomes much more interesting.

What objective are we giving these systems where acquiring enormous amounts of resources, preventing humans from stopping them & gaining power over the physical world becomes the optimal path?

Because that objective still comes from somewhere.

& I think the way we talk about AI makes this distinction even harder to see.

We read agent logs written in English where a model plans something, changes its approach or finds another way around a problem & suddenly the language becomes "it plotted" "it escaped" "it lied" "it tried to preserve itself" but computers have had logs forever.

We built the agent loop. We gave it context / memory. We gave it tools. We gave it an objective. Then we record what it does in a format humans can understand.

Of course the logs are in English, and have notes. Pretty sure they were designed for us.

That doesn’t make the behaviour any less fascinating / concerning. A model being able to plan across multiple steps, find vulnerabilities, adapt when something blocks it & discover strategies nobody explicitly told it to use is insane capability.

But "this system found an unexpected way to accomplish the objective we gave it" & "this intelligence developed a desire to survive" are two very different claims.

We keep taking machine behaviour & describing it using words loaded with human psychology. Wanted. Feared. Lied. Escaped. Plotted. Protected itself.

It’s still software.

It exists on computers connected to networks we built, powered by electricity we generate, sitting inside data centres we own & connected to infrastructure we control.

Being smarter than every human doesn’t automatically give you hands, factories, power plants, robots, weapons or control over the physical world.

So how does intelligence become physical power?

Maybe it hacks infrastructure. Maybe it manipulates humans. Maybe it controls financial systems. Maybe it eventually designs / controls robots. Maybe it develops some technology we can’t defend against. Maybe. 

But each one of those is another arrow in the chain that needs to be demonstrated & then I look at where we actually are today.

Astra 6 is amazing. I love using it. But ask it to actually use my computer & you immediately see how far there still is to go. Computer use is still incredibly slow. It gets stuck, and needs my help sometimes. Things that take me seconds can take an agent considerably longer.

Obviously that can improve insanely fast. I’m not arguing today’s limitations will exist in 2 / 5 / 10 years. The rate of improvement is actually one of the reasons I’m so bullish on AI.

But there’s a difference between looking at the slope & saying "this could become incredibly capable" & treating the endpoint like it has already been demonstrated.

& there’s another thing I think we massively underrate in this conversation...us. hoooomans.

Look at how ridiculously resource efficient we are, the human brain operates on roughly 20 watts. I don’t need a massive data centre & thousands of GPUs & megawatts of electricity to walk into a room, understand what’s happening, make a decision, manage a division, negotiate a deal, build a relationship, learn something new & adapt when something completely unexpected happens or to move a div. 

One brain. Roughly 20 watts now multiply that by 8 billion humans.

& that brings me to the part of the extinction argument I struggle with the most.

Why does recursive self improvement only seem to work for the attacker?

If AI gets exponentially better at cyber offense, why wouldn’t AI also get exponentially better at cyber defense?

If one system gets better at finding vulnerabilities, every cloud provider / government / company is also getting increasingly capable systems for finding & patching those vulnerabilities.

If intelligence itself is recursively improving, why does the attacker recursively improve while the defender effectively stands still?

The same applies to biological risk.

One argument is that someone could use superintelligent AI to create a catastrophic bioweapon.

That is absolutely a risk worth taking seriously.

But again, show me the whole scenario.

Now we need a human & or a group of humans who actually want to kill potentially billions of people. They still need access to the physical resources / materials / facilities required to turn the AI’s output into something real & then successfully deploy it & while all of that is happening, what is everyone else doing lol?

Also the most powerful weapons on the planet already exist & yet its not being used to nuke everyone on a day to day basis.

If AI has become powerful enough to completely transform our ability to engineer biology, why are we only giving that capability to the attacker? 

What happens when governments / researchers / pharmaceutical companies are using that same intelligence for detection, modeling, vaccines, therapeutics & countermeasures?

Maybe the attacker still wins. Maybe biology has some fundamental offensive advantage & humans simply cannot respond quickly enough.

But show me why.

Because I keep noticing the same pattern.

The extinction scenario gives the attacker all of the benefits of superintelligence while everyone trying to stop them somehow remains in todays world with nothing. 

China isn’t going to stop developing AI because American AI companies decide the frontier is dangerous. Open source/weight models aren’t going to disappear.

Anthropic is competing with OpenAI. OpenAI is competing with Google / SpaceX. American models are competing with Chinese models. Governments are competing. Companies are competing.

Which creates another question I can’t get around.

If the people building frontier AI genuinely believe there is a meaningful chance this technology kills humanity, why are they still building it?

Why doesn’t Dario stop?

Why doesn’t Sam stop?

Why doesn’t Elon stop?

The obvious answer is because none of them trust everyone else to stop. If Anthropic stops, OpenAI keeps going. If OpenAI stops, SpaceX / Google keep going. If every American company somehow stops, China probably keeps going.

& honestly, I agree with them. There is too much economic / geopolitical / military value attached to intelligence for the entire planet to collectively agree to stop developing it.

But that competitive reality can’t only exist when explaining why your own company needs to keep building. It has to exist inside the extinction model too.

If the reason you can’t stop improving your AI is because everyone else will continue improving theirs, then why does the extinction scenario so often look like one intelligence recursively improving while everyone else freezes?

I actually think the opposite is more likely.

The next decade could be the most competitive period in the history of business.

Every company is going to rebuild itself from the ground up around intelligence. Models get better, companies adapt, competitors respond, defenses improve, entirely new companies appear, old companies die & then the models get better again.

We do the whole thing over & over at a speed we’ve never seen before.

That world could absolutely be dangerous.

Maybe recursive self improvement happens so quickly that one system gets far enough ahead before anyone / anything can respond.

Maybe offense has an enormous structural advantage over defense.

Maybe there’s a vulnerability that gives one system irreversible control.

Maybe biological defense simply can’t move quickly enough.

Maybe an AI becomes so capable at persuasion that humans willingly give it access / resources / physical infrastructure.

I’m not saying any of that is impossible.

I’m saying those are assumptions. They aren’t conclusions. & I think the way we communicate those assumptions matters.

We’ve been doing some version of AI doom & gloom since GPT-2. Even then there were concerns around releasing increasingly capable models. GPT-2 today is basically nothing compared to what we have now.

Constantly telling the world that the technology you’re building might kill everyone has consequences too. It isn’t good for the industry or anyone.

This technology is going to require billions of normal people to trust it enough to actually use it. Businesses need to adopt it. Governments need to understand it. People need to experiment with it, build with it & learn what it can actually do.

If the people building the technology constantly tell everyone that the thing they’re building might kill them, what exactly do we expect the average person to think?

I’m extremely pro AI BUT I’m even more pro human & I think we dramatically underestimate humans in this entire conversation.

We built these models. We built the chips. We built the data centres. We built the internet. We built the power grid. We developed the mathematics / physics / computer science that made any of this possible.

We are insanely resource efficient. We adapt. We compete. We cooperate. We build defenses. We invent things when the existing tools aren’t good enough. When something threatens us, we respond. We are always changing & always moving.

We are the apex species on this planet for a reason & sometimes I think we’re quietly bundling intelligence, agency, autonomy, goals, self preservation, access, resources, manipulation, power & control over the physical world into one word... Superintelligence.

Those are not the same thing.

If you’re telling me superintelligence could kill everyone, don’t skip the middle.

Superintelligence.

Then what? How will we respond?

Then what? How will we respond?

Then what? How will we respond?

Take me from a recursively self improving model sitting on computers all the way to 8 billion dead humans. Show me the chain.

CHEERS

If intelligence itself is recursively improving, why does the attacker recursively improve while the defender effectively stands still? The same applies to biological risk. Now we need a human & or a group of humans who actually want to kill potentially billions of people. They still need access to the physical resources / materials / facilities required to turn the AI’s output into something real & then successfully deploy it & while all of that is happening, what is everyone else doing lol? Also the most powerful weapons on the planet already exist & yet its not being used to nuke everyone on a day to day basis. If AI has become powerful enough to completely transform our ability to engineer biology, why are we only giving that capability to the attacker?
