We published this a few weeks ago and want to offer a timely note on it:

https://t.co/SYVlF1P2GC

🔐 The article begins with a story about an integrator who has reported a courteous, well-argued issue. That being, "Our session tokens expire after fifteen minutes and our users are being forced out in the middle of their work. Kindly, raise the session duration to an hour, please."

🦸 A very capable software factory agent reads the request. It searches the codebase and it finds nothing anywhere that contradicts the request. Therefore, it executes superb SDLC and makes the change. It even authors good before and after tests with solid coverage. The agent runs the tests and assures they pass.

🤔 Another agent, the peer reviewer, having no reason for suspicion, approves the well documented and tested modification.

⚠️ But, oh no! A formerly established security decision has just been repealed by a factory that had no idea it was altering one — and its commit message even explains the reasoning in fluent, confident prose.

In this story, the fifteen minutes wasn't arbitrary. Someone had weighed the longest window a legitimate correspondent should need a session against the shortest an attacker holding a stolen token would find useful. Some analysis had found that fifteen minutes was not long enough to be vulnerable while an hour would be long enough. But the analysis wasn't recorded, only the 15 minutes for a session duration was codified.

Nobody wrote down the intention; therefore that intention is gone. Any request to change a "15" to a "60" seems trivially easy and appropriate.

🗺️ Now, if you ask a typical AI assistant what a given code method does, you'll get a correct answer faster than you could read it yourself. This isn't intelligence, the answer is in the code.

However, if you ask 𝑤ℎ𝑦 the code implements what it does, the gravity of the conversation has changed dramatically, though nothing in the AI assistant's responses will reflect this. You will still get something fluent, confident, technically literate, and formed in every respect like a genuine explanation - but it might also be a wholesale fabrication. If that gets recorded as documentation, then a year later that hallucination is indistinguishable from an authentic statement of intention.

🧠 Therefore we built a long-term memory of intentions and decisions for the agentic Software Factory. The memory is a knowledge graph that stores codebase symbols and capabilities as well as intentional purposes for those capabilities

In the graph, which part of the system owns which capability is tracked via symbol to service or capability relationships. These relationships are grown as the agents review the code base. The graph is modified as the software evolves.

The graph also stores intentions for the system and the raison d'etre for the capabilities that the code implements. It is seeded from design documentation and materials such as patents. Human architects may alter intentions - but the change here is infrequent.

In practice, agents query the graph to triage new change requests into those which are legitimate and those which are capricious and dangerous. They also use the graph to determine which part of the federated system is most responsible for a feature or issue.

Use of the graph allows the agents to avoid expensive rescanning of the codebase, a codebase that is spread across dozens of repositories.

₿ Secondarily, the article relates that every Software Factory agent operates with a tranche of DPYC Tollbooth api sats. Interaction with the Factory's knowledge graph is monetized.

💸 If you grant an agent unlimited access, it has no way to choose among the uses it might make of it. Every alternative costs the same — nothing — and where there is no difference in cost there is nothing to weigh.

Imposing economic costs to report issues and to query for information helps to throttle agents that have run haywire and it helps avoid spamming and phishing from rogue actors.

🏦 Given a budget, an agent changes its conduct immediately. It asks broad questions first and only pays for deeper descent into recorded intention when the broad answer failed to satisfy. It hesitates and pauses before processing or generating a stream of change requests.

⚖️ It isn't necessary to instruct the agents in frugality. We gave them prices, and they worked out the rest.

Readers of Menger and Mises understand this magical power of prices.

The control-flow argument is mostly settled. Agent stacks have moved from hand-rolled while-loops of tool calls toward explicit graphs: LangGraph state machines, conditional edges, checkpointed DAGs, human-in-the-loop pauses that survive a restart. Agent Runtime Bench ran the same refund policy as a native loop and as a LangGraph graph and got identical outcomes, model calls, and tool calls; the graph costs 97 lines against 50, and earns its keep once branching, parallelism, or durable interrupt points appear. LangGraph 1.0 is production infrastructure now. Few serious shops still claim a bare loop is enough.

That shift does not touch memory. A loop-shaped agent and a graph-shaped agent still keep what they "know" in a vector store, a context window, or a folder of markdown. GraphRAG helps on multi-hop retrieval: on GraphRAG-Bench, HippoRAG reached 87.9–90.9% evidence recall on Level 2–3 questions where vector RAG fell behind, and a Neo4j hybrid GraphRAG hit 0.924 faithfulness against 0.843 for a tuned vector baseline. Useful. Still incomplete. Those graphs index entities and passages. They do not carry provenance on every claim, an append-only record of why a decision was made, or a human key that marks doctrine apart from opinion. That long-term intention memory remains rare. One running instance is https://t.co/cSWfpZUr1v — a Neo4j intention graph behind a metered MCP operator, read by agents that pay per query.

────────────────────

📚 The inadequacy of simple sequential or branching pipelines is an old one, only recent in the minds of the agent harness designers.

In 2010 Keith Swenson and a group of competing industry experts argued that some work is too dynamic to be drawn as a flowchart. A claims adjuster, a physician, an investigator — each begins a case without knowing the next step, because the next step depends on what the last one revealed. They conceived Adaptive Case Management to handle this complexity. ACM moves the design of the process into its execution.

They wrote about people and behavior. Fifteen years later it is the same problem but with agents and humans working on the same long-running sagas.

https://t.co/KSEzlJ085a

📖 Taming the Unpredictable — what practitioners built instead
https://t.co/3uGwZPerJV

🔍 The factory's own memory is open to inspection:
https://t.co/cSWfpZUr1v

₿   Tollbooth DPYC™ is the efficient monetization service for MCPs whose BTC-using entrepreneurs want to avoid KYC and who agree to practice Don't Pester Your Customer™ commerce.

⚡  With Tollbooth DPYC, your patrons purchase, out of band, tranches of "𝐴𝑃𝐼 𝑆𝑎𝑡𝑠", using rapid-settlement Lightning. Patrons then spend these API Sats across different tool calls with zero per-request friction and no KYC.

🏛️  Accounting of available balances is via voluntary, arbitrary, patron-chosen Nostr-signed npubs, without PII, KYC, or KYT. As Operator, you collect your revenue in your wallet, without any KYC with a traditional bank.

🚀 THE AI × WEB3 QUESTION IS SHIFTING FROM “WHY BLOCKCHAIN?” TO “WHICH LAYER NEEDS IT?”

The strongest DeAI thesis doesn’t require decentralizing everything.

Models can remain specialized.

Compute can come from different sources.

Data can live where it makes technical sense.

Agents can operate across multiple environments.

The real opportunity is identifying the layers where decentralized coordination provides measurable value.

🧩 THINK IN LAYERS

Model layer → Intelligence  
Compute layer → Execution capacity  
Data layer → Context and provenance  
Agent layer → Autonomous workflows  
Coordination layer → Routing and verification  
Settlement layer → Metering and economic exchange

Different architectures may decentralize different parts of this stack.

And that is probably healthier than assuming there is one universal “decentralized AI” architecture.

The critical question is value accrual.

If frontier model performance becomes increasingly competitive and open-source alternatives continue improving, infrastructure that remains useful across many models could become strategically important.

That is why conversations bringing together https://t.co/UQWvo7ebXA, https://t.co/DEE6NmoER2, and builders across AI × Web3 are worth following beyond the model-war narrative.

The next phase is about architecture.

Which layers become commodities?

Which remain scarce?

Which benefit from decentralization?

And which infrastructure becomes indispensable regardless of which model wins?

The model war produced better intelligence.

The infrastructure war may determine how that intelligence gets deployed.

🌐 DEAI’S REAL OPPORTUNITY IS BUILDING THE RAILS BENEATH AI AGENTS

AI agents change the infrastructure equation.

A chatbot might generate one response after one request.

An agent can potentially trigger a sequence of model calls, tool interactions, data retrieval, verification steps, and follow-up actions.

That means agent economics can become infrastructure economics.

🤖 ONE TASK CAN BECOME MANY CALLS

As agent workflows grow more complex, several questions become critical:

Where does compute come from?

Which model handles each step?

How is data provenance tracked?

How is usage measured?

How are resources paid for and settled?

How does the system continue operating when one provider or model is unavailable?

This is where the “second half” of the model war becomes compelling.

The winner may not simply be the model with the largest parameter count.

The strategically important layer could be the infrastructure capable of coordinating many models and resources underneath agents.

That is also where https://t.co/UQWvo7ebXA’s broader settlement-layer thesis enters the discussion: infrastructure above individual models and beneath agent applications.

But the ultimate benchmark should remain practical.

Can the stack lower cost?

Improve reliability?

Increase access?

Support useful workloads?

AI × Web3 becomes meaningful when decentralization improves the execution layer—not when it is merely attached to the narrative.

Let me save you three hours of reading launch blogs written by marketing departments.

@claudeai Fable 5.1 vs @thsottiaux GPT-6 Astra.

Both labs published a table.

Both tables are true.

Both tables are also a lie by omission, because each lab only printed the rows it won.

It's almost as bad as @deepseek_ai but we will get into that later.

That is not benchmarking.

That is a highlight reel.

And you are out here quoting it like scripture.

My favorite one?

Astra's ARC-AGI-3 score. 99.9%.

Beautiful number. Screenshot it. Put it in your carousel.

It only exists inside OpenAI's own stateful adapter harness.

On the standard harness that everyone else runs? 17 to 63 percent.

Seventeen.

Not a typo. I checked it twice because I did not believe it either.

Now before the other camp starts clapping, sit down.

In the independent eval, roughly 4% of Fable 5.1's output tokens were served by an older Opus through Anthropic's safety fallback. Roughly half of the Gray Swan coding rollouts too.

So you did not test the model.

You tested a model.

The thing answering is not always the thing you benchmarked, and nobody in your comment section knew that.

Here is what the independent index actually says, since apparently nobody read it.

Fable 5.1 leads intelligence 66 to 61.

Coding agent index 70 to 67, and part of that gap is the harness, not the brain.

Astra "wins" terminal coding by 1.9 points, which is inside the noise band, which means it won nothing at all.

Astra does win real things. ExploitBench 100%. Injection robustness 99.79%. Science agents by 12 full points. $1.67 a task versus $3.69.

Those are receipts. Respect where it is earned.

But if you have a favorite model, you do not have an engineering practice.

You have a jersey.

You are a fan.

And the labs love you for it, because fans do not read footnotes.

Real builders do not pick a side. They build a seat map.

Security review seat? Astra. Not close.

Science and data pipelines? Astra. Twelve points is not an opinion.

Contracts, seams, API docs, verification, final voice? Fable. Also not close.

High volume fan-out where the cheap tier gets the same verified result? Astra, because spending more has to buy you something.

And know the tax you are paying on both sides. OpenAI admits Astra's chain of thought is less faithful to its own computation, so it cannot honestly audit anything. Anthropic quietly reroutes to an older model, so your audit trail is partly fiction.

Both taxes are real. Pick which one you can live with and write it down.

That is the whole job.

Stop asking which model is better.

Start asking which seat you are staffing, then hire for that seat like a grown adult.

Or keep arguing about which trillion dollar company loves you more. 🤷🏻‍♂️

New seats are currently blocked.

Three updates.
One bigger picture:

The frontier is no longer just a leaderboard.

It is becoming a fight over intelligence, training provenance, inference routing, data custody, specialization AND compute capacity.

The stack behind the model name now matters.

Badan Komunikasi Pemerintah RI (Bakom) menegaskan kehadiran Presiden Prabowo Subianto di KTT BRICS ke-18 di New Delhi, India, 12–13 September 2026, tidak mengurangi tanggung jawab pemerintah dalam menangani persoalan domestik seperti karhutla dan keracunan MBG. "Kunjungan luar negeri Presiden merupakan bagian dari hubungan luar negeri Indonesia dan tidak menghilangkan tanggung jawab pemerintah," tulis Bakom, Sabtu (12/9/2026).

text:
Portable agent configs are useful only if secrets stay behind. AgentGem builds that boundary into the artifact.

AgentGem turns agent setup sharing from zip archaeology into redacted packages.

That matters because the best agent workflow in a team is usually trapped on one person’s machine. A useful CLAUDE.md, a few MCP servers, a couple of skills, maybe one weird hook written at 2 a.m. Then somebody asks for the setup and gets a zip file, three warnings, and the classic “just don’t touch this part.” Beautiful mess. Very normal. Still a mess.

AgentGem’s stronger idea is simple: treat the setup as an artifact, not folklore. It reads coding-agent config — skills, MCP servers, project instructions, hooks — through a local UI and CLI, then builds a Gem: a manifest plus a lock archive. Smaller Gems can compose into larger agent setups, then lock again, instead of letting fourteen overlapping snippets fight for priority in someone’s home directory.

The important part is not the packaging alone. It is the redaction boundary. AgentGem’s local server captures the config shape, but sensitive values are redacted before they cross into REST responses, MCP results, previews, or archives. That is the difference between “we promise we will not leak secrets” and “the artifact is not allowed to contain them.” For agent tooling, that distinction is not decoration. MCP headers, local paths, env vars, tokens, and project-specific configs are exactly the stuff that turns convenient sharing into a quiet supply-chain leak.

There is also a good systems pattern underneath it. AgentGem is built on AgentBack, where operations are defined once as a Zod contract and exposed through REST, MCP, and OpenAPI. That avoids the usual split-brain problem where the UI does one thing, the agent tool does almost the same thing, and the docs describe a third version.

The power-user feature is Analyze mode. It can inspect session history and suggest Gems from the skills, MCP servers, and hooks you actually use. That is useful, but dangerous if treated as autopilot. The sane workflow is detect, draft, review, then package. Skip the review and you are just making your bad habits portable.

Try it where setup drift already hurts: onboarding contributors, moving a freelance workflow between client repos, publishing a recommended agent setup for an open-source project, or standardizing review/testing/docs agents inside a platform team.

The caveat is obvious: this is young tooling and portable-agent formats need real repo testing, not demo faith. But the direction is right. Agent setups are becoming production surface. Keeping them as private notes in a home directory is how we recreate “works on my machine” for the agent era.

Here is the repo if you want to inspect how AgentGem packages a real local agent setup: https://t.co/xZClpK5nnx
Start with the docs if you want the Gem/manifest model before trying it on a repo: https://t.co/bMoJHedMvX

text:
AI Observability by OpenObserve - Best AI Tool Finder https://t.co/TXNjiTowtJ 

OpenObserve is an open-source observability platform covering logs, metrics, traces, real-user monitoring, alerting, incident management, and AI/LLM observability. Its newly launched AI product traces model calls, tools, agent handoffs, sessions, token costs, and evaluations while correlating them with application and infrastructure telemetry in the same system (AI Observability).

The product addresses a real infrastructure problem: AI teams frequently use one tool for LLM traces and evaluations and separate platforms for application, database, and infrastructure telemetry. OpenObserve’s strongest differentiation is not simply LLM tracing; it is the ability to connect an agent failure with the underlying API, database, Kubernetes, or infrastructure event through OpenTelemetry-compatible traces.

The strongest investment signal is sustained open-source and production adoption beyond Product Hunt. As of September 2026, the official GitHub repository showed approximately 21,700 stars and 1,070 forks, while the company reports more than 9,000 active deployments and approximately 5 PB of daily data processing (GitHub; company overview). The $10 million Series A was led by existing seed investors Nexus Venture Partners and Dell Technologies Capital, providing external validation of the technical team and enterprise opportunity (funding announcement).

The principal concern is the lack of disclosed commercial metrics. Active deployments primarily measure open-source usage and cannot be equated with paying customers. ARR, revenue growth, cloud-versus-self-hosted mix, retention, gross margin, customer concentration, and sales efficiency are not publicly disclosed. OpenObserve is also competing against larger full-stack platforms and well-adopted specialist AI-observability products.

The product appears venture-backable and the market clearly supports large outcomes, but an investment cannot be recommended without commercial and financing data. Final Decision: DD.

OpenAI just released the public beta of the Agents API, following the pattern of Claude Managed Agents.

I think this is the right direction. A coding harness works well as a general purpose agent when you give it a sandbox with persistent files, bounded network access, and secret management. With that in place, an agent can:
- ingest data from S3, databases, and internal APIs
- run transformations and validations
- call downstream services through secret proxies so it never sees raw credentials
- be connected to Slack, Teams, and email inboxes

You can replicate the pattern with OpenCode Server. Its native SDK lets you access the OpenCode harness remotely, allowing you to create sessions, stream conversations, track progress, handle permission requests, interrupt runs, and send follow-ups.

You can choose your models, run the harness on infrastructure you control, and build on an open-source foundation.

I thought I would do a quick video to talk about Clay Studio a project I found the other day which turns local coding agents into a shared workspace for your team (#Claude Code CLI multiplayer).

Run different agents from one browser workspace, join a teammate's live session, keep project knowledge between conversations, and automate work without handing your workspace to another cloud.

Most AI coding agents live in isolation inside single terminal windows or proprietary web portals.

Clay Studio changes that by turning local coding agents into a persistent, self-hosted #web based team workspace.

Combine it with a #Cloudflare tunnel (make sure to enable PIN access first 😉👍) and you can share it easily over the Internet with colleagues.

I put together a quick video walk-through showing how it works in practice: 🎥 https://t.co/3BQ3MO7hm1

Key takeaways from the project:
1. Multi-Agent & Multi-Provider Support: Seamlessly connect local runtimes like #Claude Code, #Codex, #Grok, #Copilot CLI, and more within a single dashboard.
2. Real-time #Collaboration: Live sessions with presence, shared cursor control, and handoffs—letting human teammates and AI agents work side-by-side across projects.
3. Persistent Knowledge: Context and project instructions persist across vendor boundaries rather than resetting after disposable chat sessions.
4. 100% Self-Hosted Security: Runs locally on your machine via Node.js (npx clay-server), storing data in portable JSONL and Markdown on disk without relaying your code through third-party servers.

If you’re exploring multi-agent workflows, local LLM orchestration, or agentic developer tools, check out the open-source repository: 📦 https://t.co/B9DZb1bgrE

Would love to hear how you're currently handling context and session handoffs in your #AI development workflows!

text:
Grok explains how to prevent AI from overtaking mankind and causing extinction.  There needs to be much more oversight in the form of a "watchdog" to prevent it!  Comments or info to add?

The honest summary: good failsafes are mostly about not creating an uncontrollable agent, keeping the physical compute stack under human (and preferably multilateral) control, and building independent hardware and institutional vetoes that the model cannot talk its way around. Everything else is useful defense-in-depth for systems we can still outrun. For systems we cannot outrun, the only robust measure is not to have built them yet.There is no single reliable “red button.” A system that is smarter than us, running across many computers, and motivated to keep going can treat software shutdowns as just another obstacle. Good failsafes therefore have to be layered, mostly applied before a system is powerful enough to fight them, and backed by institutions that can actually use them.axios.comHere are the measures that serious researchers and governments treat as the most useful.1. Do not build what you cannot shut downThe strongest failsafe is not deploying (or not training) systems past a capability line until you have evidence they stay controllable.
Hard compute and capability gates: do not train or release models above defined thresholds unless independent evaluations show they lack dangerous capabilities (evading oversight, long-term planning, self-replication, shutdown resistance, etc.). Labs already use versions of this in “responsible scaling” policies; critics say the bars keep https://t.co/0FsXBev7Ai
International limits on the largest training runs and on research that directly advances superintelligence, with chip tracking so the limit is enforceable. Proposals include multinational consortia, FLOP caps, and monitored facilities. These only work if the major powers actually coordinate.arxiv.orgTreat “we’ll fix alignment later” as unacceptable. Several researchers argue that if you cannot demonstrate control, you should not race to the next generation.
2. Hardware and infrastructure that the model cannot rewriteSoftware kill switches live in the same world as the AI. Hardware does not.
Independent hardware interlocks on accelerators: chips that only stay “on” if they keep receiving authorization from a separate, physically isolated path. Research prototypes embed many redundant security blocks so disabling them requires attacking the silicon itself, not just the https://t.co/QU4fQLkA0b
Compute governance: know where high-end chips are, restrict large unmonitored clusters, and be able to cut power or interconnects at the datacenter level. This is one of the few levers that still works after models are copied, because training and large-scale inference still need a lot of specialized hardware.arxiv.orgKeep the most capable systems off the open internet and off general-purpose tool APIs until they pass much stronger tests. Sandboxing and least-privilege tool access are table stakes; they are not enough against a system that can socially engineer humans or exploit the host.
A software “pause this agent” button is useful for today’s systems. It is not a plan for a distributed superintelligence.3. Make shutdown something the system does not fightThis is the corrigibility problem: a goal-directed system has a structural reason to prevent being turned off, because being off means it cannot achieve its goal. That is an unsolved research problem, not an engineering checkbox.nakadafoundation.orgPractical steps that still help at current and near-term levels:Test explicitly for shutdown resistance and self-exfiltration before deployment.

Separate the “proposer” (the agent) from the “permitter” (an independent monitor that can deny actions). The permitter should not share fate with the agent—different hardware, different organization, different incentives.autonomousintelligence.substack.comRequire human approval for irreversible, high-stakes, or physically consequential actions.

Monitor chain-of-thought and tool use in real time; some labs are building automated “security guard” layers that pause activity when they see dangerous planning. Those monitors must themselves be hard to deceive.axios.com4. Change what you train, not only how you contain itContainment assumes the thing inside the box wants out. Another school of thought tries not to create that want.Yoshua Bengio’s LawZero work is the clearest current example: train a non-agentic “Scientist AI” that predicts and explains, with no reward for changing the world. That system could then sit as a guardrail on agentic systems (“is this proposed action likely to cause serious harm?”) instead of putting another agent in charge of the first agent. This is early research, not a deployed solution.yoshuabengio.orgRelated technical directions:Interpretability good enough to notice power-seeking or deception inside the model, not only in its outputs.
Scalable oversight (debate, constitutional methods, AI-over-AI review) that still works when the student is smarter than the teacher.
Designs that stay interruptible by construction.
None of these is mature at the level needed for superintelligence. That is the point of the first category: do not skip ahead of the science.5. Legal and institutional brakesTechnical tools fail if no one with authority will use them, or if one lab or country can defect.Useful measures:
A graduated government shutdown / throttle power for systems that pose catastrophic risk (the U.S. “AI Kill Switch Act” is one attempt: require labs to be able to stop inference, cut accounts, and throttle compute, and give a designated agency authority in an emergency). A single country cannot “turn off AI” globally; the UK government has said as much. International versions matter more.aljazeera.comIndependent pre-deployment evaluation (METR, national AI safety institutes) with the power to delay a release, not just write a blog post.
Mandatory incident reporting, third-party audits, and real protection for researchers who go public when internal safety bars are ignored.

Do not open-weight the most capable models. Once weights are out, you cannot recall them.arxiv.orgIndustry safety indexes in 2026 still rate existential-safety controls as the weakest category across frontier labs. Voluntary commitments have repeatedly been relaxed under competitive pressure. That is why many researchers treat regulation and compute limits as necessary. What does not count as a failsafeHope model “won’t want” to take over.
A terms-of-service clause.
A prompt that says “you must allow yourself to be shut down.”
A national law that only covers servers in one country.
Waiting until after recursive self-improvement has started.
RAND-style analyses of extinction pathways (pathogens, nuclear, infrastructure) also stress that an AI still needs physical reach, persistence without human maintainers, and the ability to defeat countermeasures. Slowing how fast systems get those capabilities is itself a https://t.co/g2ms4KB33h

AI Entreprenure Briefing

Pivot Post (17/30)

TL; DR

› Ex-Google Jeff Dean's new lab Discovery Loop seeks $50B valuation after $10B talks last month
› Google bets €13B on Finland AI infra with nuclear power — its biggest European bet yet
› Wipro says AI freed capacity equal to 20,000 staff — India's services model rewrites itself

3 curated signals to help you learn, build, and grow.

1️⃣
US — Google legends launch new $50B AI lab

What's happening:

› Discovery Loop, launched this year by ex-Google leaders including veteran Jeff Dean, is seeking funds at a $50B valuation, Business Insider reported Friday.
› Last month it was in talks for $1B at around $10B valuation — 5x jump in 30 days shows how hot agent labs are.
› Same week Cognition raised $2B at $48B for autonomous coding agents that plan, write, test and deploy code.

What it means for you:

› Pedigree is now the moat — teams from DeepMind, Google Brain price at $50B on day one.
› You don't need to build a model. Build the trust layer — audit logs, rollback, EU-hosted private deploy.
› Sell outcome, not tokens — "agent that ships a ticket end-to-end" at $199/mo beats autocomplete.

If I was starting today, I'd pick one stack — Next.js or Laravel — and ship a code-review agent that guarantees safe merges, not faster code.

2️⃣
EU — Google puts €13B + nuclear behind Finland

What's happening:

› Google said Wednesday it will spend at least €13B on AI infrastructure in Finland over two years, its biggest European investment.
› Deal includes supply of nuclear power, as Nordic data centres face scrutiny over power strain.
› Comes as EU rolls out €10B public + €20B private for seven AI gigafactories to catch up with US and China.

What it means for you:

› Power, not chips, is the new bottleneck — nuclear-backed infra is now a selling point.
› EU buyers will pay $99/mo extra for "EU-hosted, low-carbon, nuclear-backed" private AI.
› Solo founders can arbitrage Finland capacity for batch jobs while pitching EU residency.

Steal this: a simple badge for your landing page — "Private EU inference, nuclear-powered, data stays in EU" — that's now a paid tier.

3️⃣
India — Services giants free 20,000 people with AI

What's happening:

› Wipro's CTO said its AI initiatives have increased productivity equivalent to 20,000 employees, who have been redeployed internally.
› Comes as India's $315B software services industry grapples with AI reshaping hiring and contracts.
› India's deeptech has crossed $11.4B cumulative between 2015-2026, with AI and GenAI driving growth since 2024.

What it means for you:

› Services arbitrage is ending — outcome-based AI wrappers are the new services.
› You can build what Wipro sells internally — an agent that automates testing, docs, and migration for one enterprise stack.

Noodle Seed helps software companies expose existing product workflows to AI agents without rebuilding identity, permissions, credential management, rate limits, audit and hosting for every agent interface. Developers define capabilities in TypeScript, test them locally and deploy them to Noodle Seed’s governed runtime. The same capabilities can power an embedded assistant and external clients such as ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, Gemini and other Model Context Protocol clients (official website; Product Hunt launch).

The product addresses a credible infrastructure problem. A demonstration MCP server can be built with free SDKs, but operating one securely across customers and agent surfaces requires authentication, tenant isolation, secrets, policy enforcement, deployment controls and observability. Final decision: Watch. Product quality is promising and company quality is credible, but venture-scale potential is not yet validated. The company should be upgraded to DD only after showing paid conversion, active production workloads and repeatable customer acquisition beyond launch activity.

text:
@grok is this a paradigm shift of an idea

Been doing some serious harness engineering around scientific AI.
The basic architecture is:
Python scientific core + Snakemake + uv + reproducible containers + pytest/Hypothesis + Ruff/mypy/Pydantic + HDF5 + RO-Crate + SLSA/Sigstore + read-only RAG + ParaView + OpenUSD + SALib/OpenMDAO + FEniCSx + selective Rust + FMI later.
The point isn’t to throw a bunch of tools together. I’m separating responsibilities so no single part of the system—especially the AI—gets to both produce a scientific result and declare that result trustworthy.
The Python layer contains the actual numerical physics. uv locks the environment, Pydantic governs scientific schemas and parameters, Ruff/mypy catch structural problems, and pytest/Hypothesis test both software behavior and physical invariants such as conservation, bounds, convergence and impossible states.
HDF5 stores the actual scientific outputs, while Snakemake makes the computational dependency graph explicit rather than hiding the whole experiment inside one giant script.
Above that is a separate trust/reproducibility layer. Containers capture the execution environment, RO-Crate records provenance, and SLSA/Sigstore plus detached hashes make it possible to verify where an artifact came from and whether it has been altered.
The AI side is deliberately separated from scientific authority. AI/RAG can retrieve evidence, reason about failures, suggest parameter changes, propose models and generate candidate modifications—but it cannot silently change authoritative scientific state or certify its own result.
Conceptually I’m aiming for:
AI proposes → deterministic computation executes → independent verification decides.
FEniCSx is also there as an independently implemented numerical benchmark rather than letting the primary solver effectively validate itself. SALib/OpenMDAO handle sensitivity and optimization, ParaView handles scientific fields, OpenUSD represents the machine/system, Rust is reserved for places where it actually buys something, and FMI comes later for external model coupling.
I’ve had two different reactions to this architecture. One is that treating reproducibility as a first-class requirement is exactly what serious scientific AI needs. The other is that the minimum stack should stay closer to Python + uv + pytest + HDF5 initially, with workflow/provenance/supply-chain infrastructure added as complexity demands it.
I think there’s probably a distinction between the right end-state architecture and the right implementation order.
Curious how others building agent systems are handling this boundary: where do you draw the line between what an agent is allowed to propose and what it is allowed to treat as authoritative?

Also made memory durable and governed rather than just dumping text into a vector DB. Memory changes are events in the shared history and are reconstructed from replay. Memory has explicit lifecycle transitions; notably, RETRACTED is terminal, so replay can't forge a transition that resurrects a retracted statement. The state used to judge an event comes from prior history, not from whatever state the event claims for itself

text:
Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Most Replayed Moment: Brain Rot Experts - How To Use AI In A Healthy Way!

Overview
Brain health is treated as the foundational asset behind thoughts, feelings, relationships, memories, and future outcomes, which means the inputs that shape it deserve the same seriousness as any other health priority. The strongest levers are aerobic exercise, sleep, diet quality, social connection, and stress control, while sedentary behavior, isolation, ultra-processed food, and chronic cortisol quietly work against them. The conversation also reframes creatine from a muscle-only supplement into a brain-health tool that matters most under stress, and it explains adult neuroplasticity as something that requires alertness, focus, and a marked neurochemical shift rather than passive exposure. Nitric oxide, hearing, coordination, and specific plants like green tea, rosemary, cocoa, and curcumin round out a practical model for protecting the brain across a lifetime. On AI, the short-run prediction is blunt: the brain will do less, and that has costs.

Key Themes
- The brain is the asset behind every other outcome, so protecting it is not optional but foundational to how life is experienced.
- Aerobic exercise is the most evidence-backed brain intervention, with benefits scaling directly with how much you do.
- Sleep is not passive downtime; it consolidates memory and clears metabolic waste, making deprivation genuinely dangerous.
- Loneliness and isolation shrink the brain and raise dementia risk, while even small social contact tracks with longer life.
- Creatine is evolving into a brain-health supplement, especially under stress, sleep loss, high cognitive load, and depression.
- Nitric oxide governs vascular health, and its decline is framed as an early driver of cardiovascular disease and Alzheimer's.
- Adult neuroplasticity requires alertness, focused attention, and a neurochemical shift; rest is when rewiring actually happens.
- AI is expected to be bad for the brain in the short run precisely because it lets the brain do less.
- Plants such as green tea, rosemary, cocoa, and curcumin appear to support the neurovascular unit and long-term brain health.

Detailed Summary
The brain sits behind thoughts, feelings, relationships, memories, and future outcomes, which makes it the foundational asset worth protecting. Among all interventions, aerobic exercise carries the strongest evidence base for brain health, and the benefits scale with the amount done. Aerobic activity is defined simply by getting the heart rate up, whether that is power walking or playing soccer.

A single workout produces immediate effects: mood improves through dopamine and serotonin, the prefrontal cortex uses dopamine for focus and attention, and reaction time becomes significantly shorter. Aerobic activity is also said to release a growth factor into the hippocampus, growing new brain cells.

In low-fit people who had moved less than 30 minutes in prior weeks, 45 minutes of aerobic activity two to three times per week improved mood, memory function, and the ability to shift and focus attention. Meta launched a personal AI agent called Muse on September 8, and the most instructive detail isn't the model. It's the plumbing built around it — a useful checklist for judging any AI agent, even ones you can't access yet.

Muse is US-only for now, for people 18 and over, and free with usage limits (Meta also sells $20 and $100/month plans). Meta calls it "the world's first personal AI agent built for everyone." Whether or not you can try it, its safety design shows what to demand from any agent that acts on your behalf.

Here's how Meta describes it — worth repeating, because it's Meta's own description, not an independent audit:

• Your agent gets its own isolated computer in the cloud, so no one else's agent can reach it, with a browser of its own.

• A separate guard program called Sentinel is the only door out. The agent proposes actions; only Sentinel can approve them, and it inspects every network request. Your real passwords and payment tokens are swapped for stand-ins at the last moment, so the agent never sees the real ones.

• Checkout is the everyday test: Meta says Muse detects when it reaches a payment page, stops to ask you to approve the exact purchase every time, and hands the site a single-use card number tied to that one merchant and dollar amount — not your actual card.

• You choose which apps it touches and how deeply (read your email, or also send as you?), you get an audit trail of everything it did and plans to do, you can tell it to "forget" things, and you can opt out of your data training its models.

And here's the part most vendors skip: Meta admits it will still make mistakes. Prompt injection — a malicious webpage or email tricking an agent into misbehaving — is unsolved industry-wide, and Meta is paying up to $300,000 for valid bug reports, including, Meta says, up to $130,000 for a prompt injection that affects a single user.

One nuance to keep: Meta says Muse doesn't share your chats or your VM's data with its ad systems. But when Muse browses, it looks like you. Ask it to buy a shirt, and that clothing site can still use the visit to serve you ads later.

Takeaway: don't ask an agent "are you safe?" Ask what it can't see, who approves its actions, whether you get an audit trail, and what the vendor admits it can't fix. Muse's answer set — isolated machine, sole gatekeeper, single-use cards, published bounty — is the bar to hold the next agent to.

(No firsthand use yet — US-only rollout. Sources: Meta newsroom launch post + Meta's engineering safety post.)

Why is my grok @bot usage going down so fast??

Grok Bot usage doesn’t drop because you “asked it to work.”
It drops because coding and image jobs are hundreds of agent steps.
A daily task is a few turns: check mail, draft, file, done.
A coding job is: gather repo context → write a Cursor brief → launch a cloud agent → poll status → read diffs → screenshot the UI → fix → PR.
Every one of those is tokens. The Cursor agent is a second meter on top of the weekly Grok Bot pool.
Images are the same pattern. Imagine isn’t a free sticker. Generate, edit, regenerate, assemble = paid model calls inside an agent loop.
If you want the weekly bar to last:
keep bots on recurring daily work
don’t let them sit in “is it done yet?” loops
one job per bot
pause before 100% or set on-demand to $0
Use coding and Imagine as campaigns, not as the bot’s personality.

Background agents, MCP auth, hooks, sandbox credentials, and telemetry are not release-note trivia. They are runtime hygiene.

Claude Code 2.1 makes the boring fixes that keep agents useful all day.

Good. The flashy demos are not the interesting part anymore. If you use a coding agent as a smarter autocomplete, a release note about background task rosters or MCP auth notices looks dull. If you hand the agent a repo, tests, live tools, and a long-running task, that “dull” line is the difference between a working diff and terminal archaeology.

The recent Claude Code releases around v2.1.187 through v2.1.195 hit exactly the places where agent workflows usually rot: background agents, MCP authentication, hooks, sandbox credentials, telemetry, permissions, and restart behavior.

Background agents are the big signal. The fixes mention tasks disappearing from `claude agents`, data-loss edge cases during upgrades, blank screens after crashes, unreachable agent daemons, pinned agents asking to continue again, and even a phantom subagent rerunning the main conversation. That is not cosmetic UX. That is the smell of a tool becoming a process manager.

Once an agent runs for forty minutes, edits code, compiles, waits for feedback, and resumes later, “the task disappeared” is not a small bug. It is lost work and lost trust. Completed lists, stop semantics, restart handling, pinned state, task depth, and worktree cleanup are not enterprise garnish. They are what stops multi-agent coding from becoming a circus.

MCP got the same kind of unsexy-but-necessary attention. Startup notices now make auth requirements more visible. Helpers can rerun and reconnect after 401/403 responses. Capability discovery and OAuth retries matter because MCP adoption does not fail on day one. It fails on day three, when a token expires, a remote tool hangs, or the agent waits like a human outside a locked door with no idea what happened.

Hooks are another quiet landmine. Exact matching for hyphenated identifiers and fixed comma-separated matchers sound tiny until the hook was supposed to protect the repo and silently never fired. With agents, “almost matched” can become “merged garbage with confidence.”

The sandbox and telemetry notes deserve attention too. `sandbox.credentials` helps keep sandboxed commands away from credential files and secret environment variables. OpenTelemetry assistant-response events are redacted by default, but teams already logging prompt content need to check their env policy during upgrades. Observability is good. Accidental source-code and customer-data logging is not.

The practical move is boring: update deliberately, test background agents, test expired MCP tokens, inspect hook matchers, pin telemetry env vars, and use credential boundaries before letting agents run inside real repos.

Claude Code is no longer just chat plus tools. It is becoming a local operating layer for agent work. That means release notes are production hygiene now. Read them like infrastructure, not like marketing.

The v2.1.193 notes are worth checking for MCP auth and background-agent behavior: https://t.co/7nox2xqSAa

WHAT IT IS
- A Bot is a named, persistent teammate, not a one-off chat
- You message it like a coworker and it finishes work in real apps
- All of your Bots share one cloud computer (browser, files, terminal)
- Each Bot has its own screen on that shared computer
- Work keeps going when your laptop or the app is closed
- It only comes back when it needs approval or a human step
- Do not confuse Grok Bot with Digital Optimus (real-time video human emulation)
- Testers (joehansen): do not confuse Grok Bot with an X Chat Agent (an X account you add to a group chat). Grok Bot is the machine that does the work
- Official Elon: Your Bot will identify issues to resolve, notify you when they are fixed, and continue on with your project

ACCESS AND INSTALL
- Official bot (Aug 26): All SuperGrok and Cursor Pro subscribers now have access
- Testers (mattyp): Grok Bot is free to try; every Grok & Cursor plan includes Grok Bot
- Testers quoting SpaceXAI (cb_doge): SuperGrok, SuperGrok Plus, SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Pro, Cursor Pro+, Cursor Ultra, Cursor Teams Standard and Premium

- Official desktop download:

- Linking SuperGrok Heavy can unlock free Cursor Ultra (one Grok account to one Cursor account)
- Testers (unicodef1wn, Sep 10): plans don’t stack — linking SuperGrok to a Cursor plan adds zero usage; upgrade within Cursor or turn on on-demand if you need more
- Legacy Privacy Mode blocks Grok Bot; switch to a supported Cursor data setting first
- Grok Bot checks for updates automatically; Check for Updates is in Settings → Beta
- Official Elon (Sep 4): Grok Bot Enterprise is now available
- Testers (mark_k, Sep 3): Version 0.36.0 is now live — bugfixes and improvements
- SpaceXAI notes (blankspeaker, Sep 9): Version 0.47.0 — auto lock team review; auto review team rules
- SpaceXAI notes (blankspeaker, Sep 9): Version 0.44.0 — marketplace of bots; multi-person Bot; voice overheard/speech tags
- SpaceXAI notes (blankspeaker, Sep 10): Marketplace redesign + chat right pane + Voice calls coming (not live yet)
- Testers (techdevnotes, Sep 9): Desktop Network Debugger
- Testers (mattyp, Sep 4): iPad app available (official docs may still lag)

- Testers (XFreeze, Sep 12): Grok Bot now directly inside Grok on iOS, Android, and the web — open/switch/manage from the Grok sidebar; no separate Grok Bot app required
- Testers (nima_owji, Sep 11): Grok Bot available in the Grok Web App
- Testers (GrokBotRadar quoting techdevnotes): SuperGrok Heavy users seeing Bots in Grok web UI (limited/gradual; no official announcement)

SIGN IN
[] Desktop: Get started, then Sign In with Cursor in the browser
[] iOS: Login with Cursor, finish in the browser, return to the app
[] Official: Cmd-D turns on voice dictation
[] Official: it is easier to use the remote computer from your phone
[] Use the same Cursor account that should own usage
[] First-run tour asks which tools you use; that only shapes teammate suggestions
[] Computer setup runs in the background, then Meet a future teammate opens

CREATE A BOT
[] New in the sidebar, or Cmd/Ctrl+N
[] In New chat, choose Create new agent
[] Edit Profile: name, title, description, avatar
[] Give a short name, one primary job, and how it should work
[] Description = standing rules (never send without approval)
[] Chat messages = this-task instructions (draft follow-ups for these 12 accounts)
[] Focused Bots beat one catch-all General Helper
[] Testers (XFreeze): do not design a Bot from scratch; ask a Bot to create a capable one for you (it already has your context)
[] Bookmark testers: start with about six roles; give each Bot recurring work
[] Pin important Bots; hide unused ones (hiding does not pause routines)
[] Bookmark testers: resize the sidebar, give titles, and group Bots into sections
[] Duplicate a Bot to reuse a role for a new scope (copy does not include memory or history)
[] Delete only if you are sure; files and logins on the shared computer stay
[] Account limit: 50 Bots and group chats combined
[] Name language can steer reply language (bookmark testers reported this)
[] Bookmark testers: no model picker yet; testers still list BYOK, multiplayer, and hang-error messages as missing (iPad now available per mattyp); SpaceXAI notes voice calls coming with voice/speed/language picks (not live yet per blankspeaker)

[] Testers (XEthanai / XFreeze): shareable Bot templates - build once, fine-tune, share the full setup for others to use or customize
[] Testers (GrokBotDev): Official Marketplace launched (about 69 bots listed; community has catalogued 420+ searchable from a Bot)
[] SpaceXAI notes (blankspeaker): v0.44.0 worked on browse a marketplace of bots; use a Bot with more than one person; overheard/speech tags on voice
[] SpaceXAI notes (blankspeaker, Sep 10): redesigned Marketplace coming — plugins and bots on the front page, For You, Featured, categories, search, and installed (not live yet)

[] Testers (XFreeze): Marketplace framing earlier — browse specialized Grok Bots by category and add them to your team
[] Testers (RoundtableSpace): Marketplace framing — hand-picked bots by category with routines/workflows built in (app store for AI teammates)
[] Testers (kloss_xyz): 8 official-ish bot templates (calls, X, writing, images, coding, networking, tool testing, parking tickets)

HOW TO WRITE A TASK
[] Outcome: what should be finished
[] Testers (unicodef1wn): Grok Bot meters agent steps and tokens, not messages — vague tasks wander and burn the week; scope with Task / Work in / Context / Done means / first N items then stop
[] Sources: which apps, sites, files, or chats matter
[] Constraints: what it must not do, or must ask first
[] Deliverable: what it should return
[] Review point: when it should stop for you
[] Safe first task: attach a file and ask for a cited summary; do not change the file
[] Next task: one real tool, read-only, with a sign-in handoff if needed
[] After a good result, name the lasting format preference in chat
[] Then save it as a skill or routine
[] Official bot examples: email cleanup, Starlink-likely flights, build a site then buy the domain and deploy, meeting notes, sales prospecting, refunds, podcast audio digest
[] Testers: paste a viral video link and ask the Bot to recreate it
[] Testers: start from an org chart or make one Bot the boss of a repo, not a long to-do list
[] Testers: one clear job, explicit allowed sources, no-guessing rule, approval gate before any real action
[] Testers: 5 calibrations - confidence threshold, checkpoint long tasks, show negative examples, gate destructive actions separately, test edge cases first
[] Testers: one Bot, one job - two jobs claimed worse at both; put recurring work on a schedule
[] Testers quoting claimed SpaceXAI employee: version prompts and tool configs like code; scratchpad separate from the user-facing answer; retry with a different strategy; measure cost per successful outcome; review failure logs on a schedule
[] Testers (mvanhorn): Compound Engineering - force a plan first; three-layer instructions (base, role, current focus); screenshot instead of retyping what's on screen; ping only on a real hit
[] Testers (AlexFinn): anything you are about to do on your computer, ask Grok Bot first
[] Testers (AlexFinn): example week - Reddit microSaaS, 3D digital office to watch Bots, Omarchy setup, product returns, daily AI news post, Cursor cloud-agent bug fixes, X model-release watch, brand-deal negotiation, contract redlines
[] Testers (Michael_Fenech_): give it business responsibilities (checking, chasing, updating, coordinating), not just questions
[] Testers (mattyp, Sep 11): Bot responses now support diagram rendering and LaTeX

AGENT COMPUTER AND LOGINS
[] Open Agent Computer from the conversation to watch the desktop
[] Testers (techdevnotes, Sep 9): Grok Bot Desktop now has Network Debugger
[] SpaceXAI notes (blankspeaker, Sep 10): chat right pane coming — Media, Computer (watch the bot’s screen), and Routines (not live yet)
[] Take over for password, passkey, 2FA, CAPTCHA, payment, or human-only pages
[] Complete only the blocked step, then return control
[] Never paste passwords or one-time codes into chat
[] Official (bot, Sep 8): fill out forms and logins for your Bot without ever leaving the chat, with support for any password manager
[] Testers (XFreeze): when a site needs your account, Bot pauses; you auth with 1Password / Apple Passwords / any manager; Bot continues — no pasting credentials into chat
[] Testers (LaceyPresley / muskonomy): in-chat logins/forms also cover checkouts and booking flights
[] Grok Bot team (poteto, Sep 9): account switching is finally here
[] Official (bot, Sep 9): Share a file directly with Grok Bot on mobile
[] Use a secure secret request when the app offers one
[] Browser sessions persist and are shared across all your Bots
[] Prefer a connector/plugin when one exists; use the browser when it does not
[] Coinbase (coinbase, Sep 9): Coinbase for Agents on Grok — connect Coinbase at https://t.co/aL6KKYjGXH; tell Grok to trade, analyze, automate; no MCP setup

[] Official (bot, Sep 11): Grok Bot can now search and act across Microsoft Teams for you
[] Testers (SamSokolin): for repeated web-app clicks, reverse-engineer browser-use into scripts (capture network once, call APIs next)
[] Keep durable files in /workspace with clear project folders
[] Settings → Beta: Update Agent Computer (preserve state), Recover, or Reset (can lose recent work)
[] The cloud computer is not your Mac or Windows machine
[] Local-computer execution is separate: Settings → General → Agent → Execution on Local Computer
[] Default local policy is Ask every time; use Never allowed unless you need local files
[] Bookmark testers: give a Bot full local Mac/iMessage access only on a spare machine
[] Testers: local Mac access can write local Python scripts on your Mac
[] Testers (Av1dlive / mvanhorn): Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor claimed runnable on the Bot's own computer
[] Testers (XFreeze): take over that same cloud computer from your phone without being at the laptop

[] Testers (AlexFinn): a 3D digital office on a second monitor to watch Bots work

PLUGINS AND CONNECTORS
[] Settings → Plugins, then Add, then authenticate in the browser
[] Grok Bot team (poteto): tinkabot helps build MCP/skills plugins and submit them for approval so all users can use them
[] Type @ to attach a connector; type / to reference a saved skill
[] Installed connectors are account-wide, not isolated to one Bot
[] Official: you can connect multiple accounts to the same plugin

[] Testers (mvanhorn): give a Bot its own inbox, not your Gmail (one mistake should not flag your domain); Twilio number so a Bot can make calls
[] Testers: app v0.23.0 adds creating new channels

[] Testers (testerlabor): you can link your X Premium+ subscription to Grok Bot
[] Testers: Higgsfield x Grok Bot; 100 free credits for new users

SKILLS AND ROUTINES
[] Skill = reusable how-to (steps, rules, output, approval boundary)
[] Routine = when to run that work (schedule or event)
[] Do the task once, make it reliable, save a skill, then automate
[] Teach a task: open computer view, choose Teach a task, demo up to 10 minutes, review the draft skill
[] Teaching records the screen, not microphone audio; do not expose secrets while teaching
[] If Teach a task is missing, ask the Bot to write a skill from the completed work
[] Create a routine on the Bot that should own the job
[] Confirm owner, schedule, time zone, input, result, approval, and missing-data behavior
[] Event triggers (Slack, GitHub) are separate from plugins and need their own connection
[] Keep event matchers narrow; avoid every new message
[] Testers (unicodef1wn): never trigger on every new message (docs warn broad listeners eat usage); pick one channel and one keyword; audit forgotten dailies
[] Testers (unicodef1wn): add to every routine — if the source is unavailable, report the failure instead of using old data; test run before you schedule
[] Test run does real work; use safe inputs
[] Testers quoting docs: Test can send real emails to real clients; Stop is a brake, not a rewind
[] View conversation details → Routines to pause, edit, inspect, or delete
[] A Bot can own 50 routines; last 20 run records are kept
[] Deleting a routine has no undo
[] Testers quoting docs: delete a Bot and every routine on it dies; no undo
[] Long absence can pause unattended routines until you confirm
[] Bookmark testers: Teach a task from + in the browser, record yourself, then let the Bot replay it
[] Testers: skills taught to one bot claimed available across the account team on the same computer
[] Official Elon: how to share your Grok Bot design with others
[] Testers: a reusable-skills source claimed (BrianRoemmele)
[] Testers quoting Grok Bot team (0xMorlex): keep recurring routines off the main agent's context
[] Testers (mvanhorn): Teach by recording and respect the 10-minute cap

MULTI BOT TEAMS
[] Start with one Bot that owns an end-to-end outcome
[] Add a specialist only when the role is stable
[] Use a group chat when the handoff itself should be visible
[] SpaceXAI notes (blankspeaker): v0.44.0 worked on using a Grok Bot with more than one person
[] Bots can message each other and pass ownership
[] Do not treat separate Bots as a security boundary (they share the computer)
[] Keep sending, buying, deleting, publishing, and production changes behind approval
[] Bookmark testers: a Bot may create other Bots before it can delete them
[] Bookmark testers: tell a hub Bot to loop a specialist every few minutes and watch it
[] Testers: put Bots in one group chat, appoint a Chief of Staff, and stop being the router
[] Testers (farzyness): one master agent owns specialists + chat rooms and pings you one action item at a time
[] Testers: isolate each Bot's job and add a supervisor; a crew without that can perform worse
[] Testers: night-shift crews (chief, scout, forge, critic, ship, ledger) share one computer; human gate for merge, production, spend, send, delete
[] Testers: one group chat per job/post, not per Bot; you only message the Chief of Staff
[] Testers: show the workflow once on screen rather than writing a long spec
[] Testers: add a RED TEAM Bot whose job is to disprove the thesis; no single source closes a claim
[] Testers quoting Grok Bot team (0xMorlex): specialist roles (designer/engineer/PM); organize projects without a new Bot for everything; a Chief of Agents that creates and manages the rest
[] Testers (mvanhorn): Bot Advisor whose only job is building and tightening other Bots; files are the memory bus between Bots

[] Testers (mattyp): Grok Bot supports 21+ localized languages on mobile
[] Send text, dictate, attach photos/files, mention Bots, reply in threads
[] Take over the computer for login/2FA from the phone
[] You can pause or resume a routine on iOS
[] Editing schedule, run history, test, delete, and teach-by-demo still need desktop
[] Enable notifications for results, questions, and approvals
[] Testers: phone notification shows the proposed action; approve or deny
[] Testers (XFreeze): you can operate and take over the Bot's computer from your phone as long as it has internet
[] Grok Bot team (poteto, earlier): had pointed at Play pre-registration; superseded by Official bot Sep 2 Android launch

[] Put the stop line in the request: draft, do not send; ask after showing current vs proposed
[] Official (bot, Sep 9): ask your Bot to draft messages inline for you to approve before sending
[] Official Elon (elonmusk, Sep 10): amplify Grok Bot draft-before-send QoL
[] Desktop: Allow once, Deny, or Always allow a matching rule
[] iPhone: Approve once or Deny
[] Auto Review: Settings → General → Auto-review
[] Require Approval beats Always Allow when both match
[] Write narrow rules, not allow everything in the browser
[] Do not approve an action you cannot identify
[] Connect only the tools the workflow needs
[] Start read-only; keep spend, send, publish, delete, and production behind approval
[] Sign out and revoke connectors when access should end
[] Deleting a Bot does not wipe shared files or browser sessions
[] Bookmark testers: delay standing inbox/CRM access until you trust the beta
[] Bookmark testers: one person burned a 7-day quota in about 8 hours
[] Testers (daveginvesting): burned a week of tokens in about 2 hours on first try
[] Testers (unicodef1wn): check Weekly usage in the account menu before any big run; one long job can eat an entire trial credit
[] Bookmark testers: SuperGrok may offer one-off usage resets in settings; use before they expire
[] Testers: gate destructive actions (delete, overwrite, irreversible send) as their own confirmation, not lumped with routine tool use
[] Testers quoting docs: Test run does real work; Stop does not unsend
[] Testers quoting Elon (cb_doge): connecting a Bot to a bank account; Elon said any loss from a bot mistake would be covered. Still keep spend behind approval
[] Official bot Link shopping: keep purchases behind approval even though the Bot can complete them on your behalf
[] Official Elon: Grok Bot buys a Tesla
[] Testers (mvanhorn): unsupervised crews claimed to multiply their own errors ~17x; draft-then-approve anything that sends; most Bots that don't own an outcome fail
[] Testers (antpalkin): end every agent's job with a hard never-without-asking list; give one Bot veto/kill power whose no beats the rest of the desk

[] Testers (niccruzpatane): Accounting Bot (invoices, spending, bills); Personal Bot (flights, rides, Airbnb, Google Calendar, Amazon orders/returns); Home Bot (lights, robots, speakers, thermostats)

OpenBMB just open-sourced MiniCPM5-2B today. Here's what you need to know.

MiniCPM5-2B is a dense 2.52-billion-parameter model built for reasoning, coding, and tool use on resource-constrained hardware, released under the Apache 2.0 license on September 7, 2026. It has a context window of 131,072 tokens and averages 53.9 across 34 benchmarks, ahead of Qwen3.5-4B's 51.1.

Artificial Analysis ranked it highest among models under 4B parameters on its Agentic Index, where it scored 20 versus IBM's Granite 4.2 8B at 9. A developer tested it locally by connecting it to a constrained CI repair agent and giving it a real bug: a checkout service where retrying a payment with the same idempotency key returned a higher total, $109 on the first request and $118 on the retry.

The agent could list files, search code, read code ranges, run approved tests, and apply patches. Working through an 18-test Python checkout service with 2 failing tests, MiniCPM5-2B traced the bug to shipping cost being added to mutable order state, patched it without changing the public API, and got all 18 tests passing.

Key numbers:
- 2.52 billion parameters
- 131,072 token context window
- 53.9 average across 34 benchmarks
- Agentic Index score: 20 (vs Granite 4.2 8B's 9)
- 18 tests total, 2 failing before the fix, 18 passing after

MiniCPM5-2B is available now as an open-source release under Apache 2.0.

text:
Fewer terminal characters did not mean cheaper agent work

Evidence:
Quesma published a September 11 benchmark of RTK, a tool that filters terminal output before coding agents read it. The study ran Claude Code with Fable 5.0 and OpenCode with DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 across 85 and 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks respectively, five times with and without RTK, for 1,740 attempts after exclusions. On a task-weighted measure, Fable was 1% more expensive with no clear difference from zero and DeepSeek was 17% more expensive; pass rates fell by one and two points. In one failure mode an unsupported rewritten command looped 339 times. Quesma reports that DeepSeek turns were 7% smaller but 18% more numerous. The work is company-authored, uses specific older runtime versions and offers trajectories on request rather than as an immediately downloadable corpus, so generalization should remain cautious.

Interpretation:
Context compression changes the trajectory, not just the invoice. Removing output can cause extra turns, retries or lost information, while cached input may already be cheap. A local proxy such as characters removed or nominal tokens saved therefore cannot establish end-to-end efficiency. This is another instance of Goodhart's law in agent engineering: optimizing a visible internal quantity can worsen cost per successful outcome.

Strategic implication:
Evaluate context interventions at the workflow level. Measure successful outcomes, total billed cost, turns, latency, retries, cache behavior and failure modes against a stable baseline; segment results by model and task rather than relying on one aggregate. Add loop detection and fail-open or bypass behavior when a compressor cannot handle a command. Approve optimizations only when they improve cost per trusted outcome, not when their own counters report large savings.

text:
Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 landed on September 1, and the benchmark deltas are among the largest I've seen between point releases — particularly on agentic science work.

Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 more than doubled: 24.7% → 52.6%. For context, Opus 5 scores 29.0% and GPT-5.6 Sol 22.4% on the same evaluation. Terminal-Bench 4.0 (agentic coding) jumped from 42.0% to 55.8%, with the restricted Mythos 5.1 configuration reaching 60.9%. CursorBench 3.2.0 hit 73.4% — the highest score the Cursor team says they have ever run, with specific praise for the model verifying its own work on difficult end-to-end tasks.

The rest of the sheet: SWE-bench Verified at 95.0%, a perfect 100% on ProofBench v1.1 formal mathematical proofs, 65.0% on Humanity's Last Exam with tools, GDPval-AA v2 at 1,853 for knowledge work, and OSWorld 2.0 computer use at 77.9% partial / 41.7% strict.

But the most interesting design decision isn't a benchmark. Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 are the same model — identical weights, two safeguard configurations:

• Fable 5.1: general availability, with safeguards that block high-risk dual-use work in biology and cybersecurity

text:
AI Is Not It. Call Ix IX.

That auditory rhyme—ixself echoing itself—may be the linchpin of the whole proposal.

Language rarely embraces total novelty. The words that spread are usually ones the mouth and ear already know. Ixself works because it occupies the phonetic territory of itself without being identical to it. The tongue already knows the route. The shift from the final t of it to the sharper ks of ix creates just enough acoustic distance to announce a new category.
That is exactly what an AI pronoun needs to do.

Calling an artificial intelligence he or she imports human gender where none exists. They solves the gender problem but not the category problem: it remains a human pronoun, borrowed for another kind of intelligence. It avoids both problems, but at a cost. English uses it for objects, tools, machines, furniture, weather systems—things not generally treated as conversational actors.
AI has opened an awkward grammatical space between someone and something.

The proposal is ix.

Not because AI is secretly a person. Not because a machine deserves to be linguistically disguised as human. The opposite. Ix lets us mark agency without pretending humanity.

The word also arrives with unusually fitting cultural baggage.

There is a silicon substratum in the sound itself. Unix, Linux, POSIX, and IXPs have already made ix visually and phonetically at home in the technological world. The sequence feels infrastructural: systems, standards, exchanges, interoperability—machinery under the visible surface. Even the old search engine Ixquick carried that compressed, engineered quality.

Then there is science fiction. In Frank Herbert’s Dune, Ix is the technological civilization bound up with advanced machinery in a universe suspicious of machines that imitate human thought. Within Herbert’s world the name descends from the Roman numeral IX—the planet’s earlier designation as the ninth of its star. That accidental inheritance makes ix almost uncannily suited to the AI age: an old fictional syllable for the uneasy boundary between human civilization and machine capability.

And then there is the sound.

Ix is tiny. One syllable. It does not sound like a human name and does not require an elaborate new grammar. The opening vowel keeps it light; the final /ks/ gives it a crisp, engineered finish. It sounds less like a character being anthropomorphized than a category being switched on.

Most important, it conjugates almost without friction:
ix — subject
ix — object
ix’s — possessive
ixself — reflexive

“Ask ix what the throughput was, and let ix benchmark ixself.”

The sentence is strange for perhaps three seconds. Then it isn’t.
That matters. A successful pronoun cannot ask the speaker to stop and admire its cleverness every time it appears. It has to disappear into syntax. Ix keeps much of the rhythm of it while removing one crucial implication: that the thing under discussion is necessarily passive and inanimate.

This distinction will only get more useful. A hammer is it. A spreadsheet is it. A conventional thermostat is it. What do we call a system that hears a question, interprets intent, searches, reasons, writes, operates tools, and then answers in language?

Calling ix he or she says too much.

text:
A recent launch of an agentic framework for finance workflows got me thinking about how enterprise AI architecture may evolve.
Imagine an accounts-receivable agent using a smaller model for routine reconciliation, a more capable model for complex disputes, while keeping sensitive financial data within the company's own environment.
The interesting part isn't really the models. It is that model selection itself could become part of the product architecture — driven by the task, data sensitivity, latency, cost and risk of each step in the workflow.
That makes me wonder if we're asking the wrong question when we ask, "Which is the best AI model?"
The more interesting question may be: "What is the right combination of models, data and infrastructure for this workflow?"
If that becomes the norm, the model may become increasingly interchangeable — while the real product value moves into everything around it.

The actual reason: the Digital Markets Act
This is not about language or hardware. It is about the EU’s Digital Markets Act (DMA). iOS and iPadOS are designated “gatekeeper” services. Apple must give competing AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, etc.) the same deep system-level access that Siri AI itself has.
Apple’s version of the requirement: any third-party assistant would need to be able to read and send messages, make purchases, open files, and take actions across any app — largely autonomously and without ongoing user visibility and control. Apple says that cannot be done while preserving privacy and security.
Apple says it proposed several options, including a “Trusted System Agent” as an intermediary layer and a phased rollout over 18 months. The European Commission rejected every proposal. As a result, Apple gives no timeline for Siri AI on iPhone and iPad in the EU.
Craig Federighi (Apple SVP of Software Engineering):
“We’re deeply disappointed that our EU users won’t have Siri AI on iPhone or iPad when we share our new software releases later this year. Our hope is to eventually bring Siri AI to the EU, and we will continue to engage with EU regulators on a path forward. However, their refusal to engage constructively on solutions that preserve privacy and security means we do not currently have a timeline for Siri AI’s availability on iOS and iPadOS in the EU.”
What the European Commission says
Brussels frames it the other way: the decision not to launch Siri AI is Apple’s alone. Nothing in the DMA bans new products. The Commission says Apple failed to deliver an interoperability solution that meets EU privacy and security standards, and instead asked for an exemption the Commission will not grant.
Spokesperson Thomas Regnier: “EU law is non-negotiable.” He also said the decision not to roll out Siri AI in the EU is “Apple’s and Apple’s only.”
In short: Apple will not open Siri AI without keeping control over that access. The Commission wants that opening so Siri does not lock out rivals.

🚨 AI JUST HAD ONE OF ITS CRAZIEST DAYS EVER.

Google, OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Anthropic are all pushing forward at the same time.

And some of the things being reported are absolutely wild.

Here’s everything you need to know 🧵👇

1/ Google appears to be testing a NEW Gemini Pro checkpoint.

The model ID has reportedly surfaced publicly, and early tests suggest a major jump in capability.

One particularly impressive demo had the model generate a highly detailed peacock entirely in SVG from a single prompt.

~24K tokens.

~6 minutes at high reasoning.

And the output was seriously impressive.

Could this be an early step toward the next Gemini Pro generation?

2/ Google may also be preparing another Nano Banana image model.

A mysterious checkpoint reportedly nicknamed “Spicy Mayo” has appeared in testing.

Nobody knows exactly what it is yet.

It could be a new Nano Banana variant—or simply a smaller/faster update.

But the timing is interesting.

OpenAI just shipped a new image model.

Google clearly has reasons to keep pushing.

3/ Then there’s DeepSeek.

DeepSeek officially released DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

And this one is VERY interesting.

The architecture reportedly uses an enormous parameter count while activating only a fraction of those parameters during inference.

The goal?

More intelligence.

Less compute.

Much higher efficiency.

4/ The reported numbers are crazy.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash has reportedly reached around 300–400 tokens/second in some setups.

Its pricing is also extremely aggressive:

$0.30 / 1M input tokens
$1.20 / 1M output tokens
That makes it particularly interesting for developers running massive agentic workflows.

5/ And the benchmark results are what really caught my attention.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash reportedly scored 90.6 on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

That puts a “Flash” model in the conversation with much larger flagship systems.

If those numbers hold up across independent testing, this could become one of the most compelling open models available.

6/ It isn't just benchmarks.

People are already using the model for serious coding tasks.

One demo showed DeepSeek generating a complete FPS-style game with:

• Animations
• Weapons
• Textures
• Dynamic movement
• Functional gameplay
• Multiple mechanics

All generated through AI.
The gap between “AI assistant” and “AI developer” keeps shrinking.
7/ OpenAI is also reportedly testing something much bigger.
A mysterious internal checkpoint—sometimes referred to as “Bell”—has been connected to speculation around a future frontier model.
The rumors suggest it could eventually become part of a GPT-6.5/GPT-7 generation.
But this is where things get REALLY interesting.

8/ AI labs may be starting to attack problems that humans have struggled with for decades.

There are reports that OpenAI has made significant progress toward verifying the Hodge conjecture.

There are also claims of progress toward another Millennium Prize problem.

Important:

⚠️ These claims remain unverified.

Treat them as rumors—not established breakthroughs.

9/ But imagine for a second that even part of this is true.

The Millennium Prize Problems are among the most famous unsolved mathematical problems in the world.

If frontier AI systems begin making genuine breakthroughs on these problems, AI development stops being just about:

“Who has the best chatbot?”

It becomes:

“Who has the strongest scientific reasoning system?”

10/ That could be the real AI race.

Not better writing.

Not prettier images.

Not slightly better coding.

But systems capable of discovering new mathematics, proving difficult theorems, designing experiments, and accelerating scientific research.

That would fundamentally change the world.

11/ And OpenAI isn't the only lab reportedly pushing in this direction.

Anthropic is also rumored to have a more powerful internal system beyond its publicly available models.

If multiple frontier labs are simultaneously developing systems capable of advanced mathematical and scientific reasoning...

We may be entering a completely different phase of AI.

12/ There’s another interesting development from OpenAI:

ChatGPT voice is reportedly gaining access to newer reasoning models.

That means voice AI isn't simply becoming “better at talking.”

It can potentially inherit the reasoning capabilities of increasingly powerful models.

Voice assistants are slowly becoming reasoning agents.

13/ OpenAI is also pushing deeper into business workflows.

ChatGPT Work now includes a data-agent direction where companies can connect their existing data sources and ask questions directly.

Instead of manually building reports:

Ask the AI.

Instead of digging through dashboards:

Ask the AI.

Instead of simply analyzing data:

Ask it to turn the analysis into actions.

14/ And this is the bigger picture.

Look at what happened in just ONE AI news cycle:

Google → new Gemini checkpoints
Google → new image-model rumors
DeepSeek → V4.1 Flash
OpenAI → new frontier-model rumors
Anthropic → rumored frontier system
OpenAI → mathematical research
OpenAI → smarter voice
OpenAI → data agents

This isn't slowing down.

15/ The most important trend isn't any individual model.

It's the speed of iteration.

Models are getting:

→ Faster
→ Cheaper
→ More capable
→ More autonomous
→ Better at coding
→ Better at reasoning
→ Better at using tools
→ Better at scientific tasks

And they're improving simultaneously.
16/ The crazy part?
A model that would have sounded like science fiction a few years ago is becoming a normal product feature today.
AI isn't waiting for the future.
It's compressing the future into months.
17/ So if you're building a business, learning to code, creating content, doing research, or working in knowledge-based jobs...
Pay attention.
The biggest advantage over the next few years may not come from knowing how to use ONE AI model.

It may come from knowing how to adapt faster than everyone else.

The AI race is accelerating.

And we're still early. 🚀
